questions.stem: (I=PAT Calculation) Assuming Environmental Impact (I) is held constant, if the Population (P) increases by 50% and Affluence (A) doubles, by what factor must technology (T) reduce its impact (decoupling)?
questions.explanation: Formula: required reduction of T = P multiplier x A multiplier. P +50% = x1.5; A doubles = x2. Then 1.5 x 2 = 3.0. Adding (0.5 + 2 = 2.5 or 1.5 + 2 = 3.5) or multiplying by 0.5 instead of 1.5 (0.5 x 2 = 1.0) are the classic mistakes [M3 s17, s19].

questions.stem: (I=PAT Calculation) With Environmental Impact (I) kept constant, Population (P) grows by 25% and Affluence (A) grows 3.2 times. Technology (T) must reduce its impact by approximately what factor?
questions.explanation: Formula: factor = P multiplier x A multiplier. P +25% = x1.25; A = x3.2. 1.25 x 3.2 = 4.0. Dividing (3.2 / 1.25 = 2.56), ignoring P (3.2) or adding (1.25 + 3.2 = 4.45) are wrong [M3 s17, s19].

questions.stem: (I=PAT Calculation) Assume today's Environmental Impact (I) is 100. Population (P) increases by 40% and Affluence (A) increases 2.5 times, but technology (T) only improves its impact per unit by a factor of 2 (halved). What will the Environmental Impact (I) be, relative to today?
questions.explanation: P x A = 1.4 x 2.5 = 3.5 (I would be 350 with T constant). Technology halves the impact per unit, so I = 3.5 / 2 = 1.75 x 100 = 175. To keep I at 100, T would have had to fall by 3.5. 3.5 ignores T; 0.57 inverts the ratio (2 / 3.5); 1.5 subtracts (3.5 - 2) [M3 s17, s19].

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Kerala Data) According to the 2022 population data in the sources (Germany 242, Indonesia 141 persons per km2), what is the difference in population density between Germany and Indonesia?
questions.explanation: Formula: difference = density(A) - density(B). 242 - 141 = 101 persons per km2. 141 and 242 are single densities; 383 adds instead of subtracting [M3 s14].

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Kerala Data) Using the 2022 data in the sources, what is the approximate difference in population density (per km2) between the State of Kerala (860) and India as a whole (488)?
questions.explanation: Formula: difference = density(A) - density(B). 860 (Kerala) - 488 (India) = 372 per km2. 719 is Kerala minus Indonesia, 488 is India's own density, and 1,348 comes from adding [M3 s14].

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Kerala Data) Using the 2022 data in the sources (Kerala 860, India 488, Indonesia 141 persons per km2), how much denser is Kerala than the simple average density of India and Indonesia?
questions.explanation: Step 1: average = (488 + 141) / 2 = 314.5 per km2. Step 2: 860 - 314.5 = 545.5 per km2. 719 and 372 each use only one country; 314.5 is the average itself, not the difference [M3 s14].

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Overconsumption) A 100-watt light bulb is left on unnecessarily for 10 hours per day (an example of Overconsumption). If the electricity rate is Rp1,000 per kWh, what is the approximate cost of this waste over a 30-day month?
questions.explanation: Formula: cost = kW x hours/day x days x price per kWh. 100 W = 0.1 kW. 0.1 kW x 10 h x 30 d x Rp1,000 = Rp30,000. Rp3,000 forgets the 30 days; Rp1,000 forgets hours and days; Rp30,000,000 forgets to convert W to kW [M3 s33].

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Overconsumption) A hostel leaves 5 fans (each 60 watts) running for 8 hours per day when nobody is in the rooms. If the electricity rate is Rp1,500 per kWh, what is the approximate cost of this waste over a 30-day month?
questions.explanation: Formula: cost = kW x hours/day x days x price per kWh. 5 x 60 W = 300 W = 0.3 kW. 0.3 x 8 h = 2.4 kWh/day; x 30 d = 72 kWh; x Rp1,500 = Rp108,000. Rp3,600 forgets the days; Rp54,000 uses 4 h; Rp108,000,000 forgets W to kW [M3 s33].

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Overconsumption) A shop leaves 50 LED light bulbs (each 12 watts) on for 16 hours per day unnecessarily. If the electricity rate is Rp1,500 per kWh, what is the approximate cost of this waste over a 30-day month?
questions.explanation: Formula: cost = kW x hours/day x days x price per kWh. 50 x 12 W = 600 W = 0.6 kW. 0.6 x 16 h = 9.6 kWh/day; x 30 d = 288 kWh; x Rp1,500 = Rp432,000. Rp8,640 is one bulb only; Rp216,000 uses 8 h; Rp432,000,000 forgets W to kW [M3 s33].

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Ecological Footprint) The footprint of a country's average lifestyle is 250% of its biocapacity. If everyone in the world lived like this, approximately how many Earths would be needed?
questions.explanation: Formula: Earths needed = footprint / biocapacity = percentage / 100. 250% / 100 = 2.5 Earths (100% = one Earth). 0.4 inverts the ratio (100/250); 1.5 subtracts 100%; 25 mis-places the decimal [M3 s38, s41].

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Ecological Footprint) A country has a biocapacity of 0.9 gha and an ecological footprint of 2.7 gha per person per year. What is its ecological balance?
questions.explanation: Formula: ecological balance = biocapacity - footprint. 0.9 - 2.7 = -1.8 gha per person per year; negative means a deficit (overshoot), as for Indonesia (1.2 - 1.8 = -0.6) on [M3 s40]. A positive sign reverses the subtraction, 3.6 adds, and 0.33 is the ratio 0.9 / 2.7.

questions.stem: (Calculation based on Ecological Footprint) In the 2022 'how many Earths' data, the USA needs 5.1 Earths and the world average is 1.75 Earths. About how many times higher is the USA's footprint than the world average?
questions.explanation: Formula: ratio = A / B. 5.1 / 1.75 = 2.91, so about 2.9 times. 0.34 inverts the ratio; 3.35 is the difference (5.1 - 1.75) in Earths, not a ratio; 6.85 adds [M3 s41].

questions.stem: Refrigerant HCFC-22 has a GWP of about 1,800 (CO2 = 1). If 4 kg of HCFC-22 leaks from an air conditioner, how much is emitted in CO2-equivalents?
questions.explanation: Formula: CO2e = mass of gas x GWP. 4 kg x 1,800 = 7,200 kg CO2e (7.2 t). 450 divides instead of multiplying (1,800 / 4), 1,804 adds, and 7.2 kg is a unit slip (tonnes/kg) [M6 s6, s28].

questions.stem: According to the 2019 sector data (IPCC 2023; total about 59 GtCO2-eq: Energy 20, Industrial 14, AFOLU 13, Transportation 8.7, Building 3.3 Gt), what share of global GHG emissions came from Industrial and AFOLU together?
questions.explanation: Formula: share (%) = sector emissions / total x 100. (14 + 13) / 59 = 27 / 59 = 45.8%, about 46% (24% + 22% on the slide). 27% forgets to divide by the total; 54% is everything except these two; 58% is Energy + Industrial [M6 s32].

questions.stem: A hotel uses 800 MWh of energy per year. If cooling can use 50-60% of a building's total energy, roughly how much energy does the hotel spend on cooling per year?
questions.explanation: Formula: cooling energy = building energy x cooling share. 800 x 0.50 = 400 MWh and 800 x 0.60 = 480 MWh. 50-60 treats the percentage as MWh; 320-400 uses 40-50%; 1,333-1,600 divides by the share (800 / 0.6, 800 / 0.5) [M6 s28].

questions.stem: In Week 3 calculation questions, which formula gives the cost of running an appliance for a month?
options: Cost = power (W) x hours per day x price per kWh, because the number of days is already included in the tariff
Cost = power (kW) x hours per day x number of days x price per kWh, after converting watts to kW
Cost = power (kW) + hours per day + days + price per kWh
Cost = price per kWh / (power in kW x hours x days)
questions.answerText: Cost = power (kW) x hours per day x number of days x price per kWh, after converting watts to kW
questions.explanation: Electricity cost is multiplicative: kW x h/day x days x price per kWh, e.g. 0.3 kW x 10 h x 30 d x Rp1,000 = Rp90,000; watts must first be divided by 1,000. Adding the terms, inverting the ratio or dropping the days are all wrong [M3 s33].

questions.stem: IPAT's T (Week 3), Science, Technology and Innovation (Week 5) and Responsible Innovation (Week 7) all belong to which cross-cutting theme?
options: Commons and their governance (Ostrom, Montreal, Subak)
Limits of the planet: carrying capacity and overshoot
SDGs as a connected system of goals
questions.explanation: These concepts all deal with technology raising or cutting impact; the hub links IPAT, rebound effects, STI and RI. [M3 s16; M5 s23; M7 s19]

questions.stem: The theme 'Equity: Global North vs South' brings together the following concepts from different weeks, except:
questions.explanation: Jevons paradox is about efficiency gains raising total consumption and belongs to the technology theme. [M3 s22, s24; M4 s6; M6 s16; M7 s3]

questions.stem: Week 3 stresses the dual role of technology. Which Week 7 finding illustrates the 'worsening' side of that role?
options: Technology automatically lowers the material footprint at every income level, so SDG 12 is advanced by technology alone
Technology use is unrelated to SDG 12 and to the material footprint
Technology use raises the material footprint, hindering SDG 12 (targets 12.2, 8.4)
Renewable energy never affects any other SDG, so no trade-offs arise
questions.answerText: Technology use raises the material footprint, hindering SDG 12 (targets 12.2, 8.4)
questions.explanation: Slide 15 of Week 7 links technology to a rising material and environmental footprint (inverted U with income); Week 3 lists increasing consumption and pollution as the worsening side. [M3 s21; M7 s15]

questions.stem: Week 4 warns that technology (fences, data, energy, intellectual property rights) can privatise and fragment commons. What does it say decides whether technology strengthens or weakens collective management?
options: Clear goals and regulation that protect shared value
The speed at which the technology is adopted by the community
Whether the technology is energy-efficient or not
How many patents each individual user holds
The size of the shared resource in hectares
questions.answerText: Clear goals and regulation that protect shared value
questions.explanation: Without clear goals and regulation, technology becomes a tool of privatisation; this echoes Week 3's dual role of technology. [M4 s32; M3 s21]

questions.stem: Week 3 shows that the richest 10% emit about half of global CO2 while the poorest 50% emit only about 10%. Which Week 6 Paris Agreement principle responds to such inequality?
options: Sovereignty, embodied in bottom-up NDCs set by each country
Transparency, embodied in the Global Stocktake every five years
The goal of net zero emissions by 2060 for every country
Kyoto-style top-down emission targets with no role for developing countries
questions.explanation: CBDR-RC acknowledges that all countries contribute to climate change to differing degrees and that developed countries commit more according to ability to pay. [M3 s30; M6 s16]

questions.stem: Week 4 says the North/South split is socio-economic, not geographic. Boar et al. (2021, Week 7) report that SDG synergies in the Global South typically cover:
options: Only one dimension; North synergies span social, economic and environmental dimensions
All three dimensions, exactly as in the Global North
No dimension at all, since the South has no synergies
The social and environmental dimensions but never the economic one
questions.answerText: Only one dimension; North synergies span social, economic and environmental dimensions
questions.explanation: Boar et al.: Global North synergies cover all three dimensions; Global South synergies cover only one. [M7 s17; M4 s6]

questions.stem: Week 4 links three routes of regulating or paying for commons to cases. Which pairing is correct?
options: Subak irrigation: regulation imposed by the national government
Vehicle emissions: customary agreement among villagers under adat
Cidanau: an international treaty on ozone-depleting substances
Montreal Protocol on ozone: global mutual consent (treaty)
questions.answerText: Montreal Protocol on ozone: global mutual consent (treaty)
questions.explanation: Ozone = global mutual consent/treaty, Subak = community rules, vehicle emissions = government regulation, Cidanau = payment for ecosystem services. [M4 s18, s21, s24]

questions.stem: The Barambang Katute customary forest (Week 2) and the Subak irrigation system (Week 4) both illustrate that:
options: Shared resources always collapse unless they are turned into private ownership
Customary rules cannot work for renewable resources managed by a community
Only international treaties can stop overuse of shared resources
Commons governed by community rules can be sustained, so the problem is unmanaged open access
Open access is the best way to share a resource fairly
questions.answerText: Commons governed by community rules can be sustained, so the problem is unmanaged open access
questions.explanation: Both are defined communities with boundaries, rules and exclusion of harmful uses, answering Week 2's question 'Does the tragedy lie in the commons?'. [M2 s5; M4 s24, s31]

questions.stem: In Week 3, the ecological footprint exceeding biocapacity (overshoot) is described as the footprint version of which Week 2 idea?
options: A social shortfall below the doughnut's inner ring
Transgressing planetary boundaries, i.e. leaving the safe operating space
Reaching the plateau of the S-curve at carrying capacity
The commons being managed by a community with clear boundaries
questions.answerText: Transgressing planetary boundaries, i.e. leaving the safe operating space
questions.explanation: Biocapacity is effectively carrying capacity in area units and overshoot parallels breaching planetary boundaries. [M3 s38; M2 s6, s7]

questions.stem: Which set of figures from the slides is correct?
options: 73% of biocapacity used in 1961 and 160% in 2020; 7 of 9 planetary boundaries transgressed in 2025
Humanity used 160% of biocapacity in 1961 and 73% in 2020; 7 of 9 boundaries were transgressed in 2025
Humanity used 73% of biocapacity in 1961 and 160% in 2020; 3 of 9 boundaries were transgressed in 2025
Humanity used 100% of biocapacity in 1961 and 160% in 2020; 9 of 9 boundaries were transgressed in 2025
questions.answerText: 73% of biocapacity used in 1961 and 160% in 2020; 7 of 9 planetary boundaries transgressed in 2025
questions.explanation: Week 3: 73% (1961) to 160% (2020, about 1.6 Earths). Week 2: 7 of 9 transgressed in 2025; only 3 were crossed in the 2009 diagram. [M3 s38; M2 s6, s7]

questions.stem: Week 7 says the SDGs are not achieved one by one 'like an ivory tower'. On which three features does the 2030 Agenda's mandate rest?
options: Sovereignty, transparency and equity (the Paris principles)
Bearable, equitable and viable (the IUCN overlaps)
Mitigation, adaptation and finance (the Paris goals)
questions.explanation: Slide 6 of Week 7: transformative, universal and indivisible. The other options are the Paris principles (Week 6), IUCN Venn overlaps (Week 1) and Paris goals (Week 6). [M7 s6; M6 s14; M1 s13]

questions.stem: The 17 SDGs (Week 5) are interlinked. In the SDG wheel of the Food-Energy-Water nexus (Week 7), which three goals form the inner ring?
questions.explanation: The inner ring is food security (SDG 2), water security (SDG 6) and energy security (SDG 7). [M7 s22; M5 s4]

questions.stem: Sustainability should be understood as an open-ended, positive and temporary concept. It is called open-ended because:
options: It was fixed scientifically once and for all by the Brundtland Commission.
It applies only to environmental issues, since the economic and social dimensions are handled elsewhere.
The social understanding of sustainable development depends on time and situation, as well as culture and knowledge.
It stops being relevant once the SDGs are achieved in 2030, because all needs will then be met.
questions.answerText: The social understanding of sustainable development depends on time and situation, as well as culture and knowledge.
questions.explanation: Slide 11 says sustainability cannot be fixed once and for all: its social understanding changes with time, situation, culture and knowledge. [M1 s11]

questions.stem: On the Hopwood et al. (2005) chart of views on sustainable development, which of the following is placed under the 'status quo' view?
options: World Bank, OECD and neo-liberal economists
Social ecology and indigenous/Global South movements
Anti-capitalist movement and environmental justice groups
questions.answerText: World Bank, OECD and neo-liberal economists
questions.explanation: On the chart on slide 11, World Bank, OECD, WBCSD and neo-liberal economists sit at the status quo end, while deep ecology, social ecology and similar movements are at the transformation end. [M1 s11]

questions.stem: Which figure is credited on slide 12 with calling for the 'continuous, stable and sustainable utilization of forests' in 1713?
options: Gro Harlem Brundtland, chair of the WCED
Garrett Hardin, author of a famous 1968 article in Science
Hans Carl von Carlowitz, a German mining director
questions.answerText: Hans Carl von Carlowitz, a German mining director
questions.explanation: The 1713 call for sustainable forest use is attributed to the German mining director Carl von Carlowitz. [M1 s12]

questions.stem: The timeline of the sustainability concept on slide 12 includes the following, except:
options: The German Advisory Council divided sustainable development into responsibilities to the natural environment, the social world and to itself (1994)
Carlowitz introduced the safe and just space between a social foundation and an ecological ceiling
Boulding, Ayres & Kneese, Georgescu-Roegen and Daly put nature back on the economic agenda (1960s)
Malthus identified the imbalance between a habitat's resources and its population and predicted famines, epidemics and wars
questions.answerText: Carlowitz introduced the safe and just space between a social foundation and an ecological ceiling
questions.explanation: The safe and just space belongs to Raworth's Doughnut Economics (slide 14), not to the historical timeline on slide 12. [M1 s12, s14]

questions.stem: Which report, published by the World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), is the source of the most frequently quoted definition of sustainable development?
questions.explanation: The Brundtland Commission (WCED) published Our Common Future, which details the concept of sustainable development and the interdependence of environment, economy and society. [M1 s12]

questions.stem: A government meets this year's water demand by exhausting an aquifer on which future generations will depend. Based on the Brundtland definition, this policy is:
options: Not sustainable, because it compromises the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
Sustainable, because the needs of the present generation are fully met and the aquifer may recover in theory
Sustainable, as long as it is profitable in the short term
Irrelevant, because the definition only covers the environmental dimension
questions.answerText: Not sustainable, because it compromises the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
questions.explanation: The definition (reused for the economic dimension) requires meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs. [M1 s12, s13]

questions.stem: In the IUCN Venn diagram of the three dimensions of sustainability, the overlap of the Social and Economic circles is labelled:
questions.explanation: Social ∩ Environment = Bearable, Social ∩ Economic = Equitable, Environment ∩ Economic = Viable, all three = Sustainable. [M1 s13]

questions.stem: Slide 15 adds a nuance to the three dimensions: the environment is not just one equal circle among three. What does it say?
options: The economy is foundational and the environment is just a resource to be priced.
The environment is foundational; societies and economies depend on it and must operate within planetary boundaries.
Environmental loss can always be offset by economic gains as long as GDP keeps growing, so the three circles are fully tradable.
The environment matters only after social needs are met.
questions.answerText: The environment is foundational; societies and economies depend on it and must operate within planetary boundaries.
questions.explanation: Slide 15 calls the environment foundational and says it includes both living and non-living things (air, water, sunlight). [M1 s15]

questions.stem: In Kate Raworth's Doughnut Economics, the outer circle (the ecological ceiling) is made up of:
options: Social shortfalls such as lack of water, food, health, education, housing and political voice
The economic, social and environmental dimensions of the IUCN Venn diagram
Planetary boundaries such as climate change, biodiversity loss and ocean acidification
questions.answerText: Planetary boundaries such as climate change, biodiversity loss and ocean acidification
questions.explanation: The doughnut's outer circle is the ecological ceiling whose segments are the planetary boundaries; the inner circle is the social foundation. [M1 s14; M2 s7]

questions.stem: In a society everyone has enough food, water and housing, but climate change and biodiversity loss extend beyond the outer circle of the doughnut. In Doughnut Economics this situation is called:
questions.explanation: Red wedges beyond the outer ring are overshoot of the ecological ceiling; red wedges inside the inner ring are shortfall of the social foundation. [M1 s14]

questions.stem: Which law of ecology says that waste and pollution do not disappear but are only moved from one place to another?
options: Every element is connected to everything else
Every species depends on every other species
There is no such thing as a free lunch
questions.explanation: Law 3 on slide 18: matter is not destroyed, so wastes such as plastics or CO2 simply go somewhere else. [M1 s18]

questions.stem: The six laws of ecology on slide 18 include the following, except:
options: The laws of thermodynamics apply: energy is conserved but degrades with every transfer
There is no such thing as a free lunch: every gain from nature has a cost somewhere
Resources grow arithmetically while population grows geometrically
questions.answerText: Resources grow arithmetically while population grows geometrically
questions.explanation: The arithmetic-versus-geometric growth statement is Malthus's argument (Week 3), not one of the six laws of ecology. [M1 s18]

questions.stem: According to the Dominion thesis, nature is valuable:
options: In itself, independently of any human use
Only as long as it has benefits for humans
Because humans and nature form one moral community
Only when it is left completely untouched
questions.answerText: Only as long as it has benefits for humans
questions.explanation: The thesis holds that humans are a separate and superior entity and that nature is only useful as long as it benefits humans. [M1 s24]

questions.stem: The 17th-century wolf eradication programme, one of the first environmental regulations passed in North America, is used on the slides to illustrate:
options: Stewardship, the moral responsibility to protect the environment
The Land Ethic of Aldo Leopold
questions.explanation: Slide 24 uses the wolf eradication programme to show humans using nature however they deem beneficial, the Dominion thesis. [M1 s24]

questions.stem: Anthropocentrism is the ethical viewpoint that:
options: Ecological interests must be above the interests of the human species
The value of something is measured by its benefits, maximizing individual or societal welfare
Humans are the primary factor in determining whether actions toward nature are right or wrong
Humans have a moral responsibility to protect the environment and living things
Nature should be managed primarily for protection and preservation for the benefit of wildlife
questions.answerText: Humans are the primary factor in determining whether actions toward nature are right or wrong
questions.explanation: Slide 25 gives this definition; the other options describe ecocentrism, utilitarianism, stewardship and Muir's preservationism. [M1 s25, s26, s28, s30]

questions.stem: Opponents of agricultural industrialisation give two arguments: (A) animals are not 'capital' but sentient beings; (B) industrial farms pollute water, disrupting human health downstream, and shut down small traditional farms. Which one is human-centred (anthropocentric)?
options: Argument A, because it treats animals as sentient beings and not as 'capital'
Both, because every ethical argument is ultimately made by and for humans
Argument B, because the harm is judged by its effect on humans
Neither, because ethics is never human-centred
questions.answerText: Argument B, because the harm is judged by its effect on humans
questions.explanation: Slide 22 asks exactly this: Argument B concerns human health and livelihoods, while Argument A gives sentient animals moral weight. [M1 s22]

questions.stem: Gifford Pinchot's conservationist ethic aims at:
options: Protecting nature from use, for the benefit of wildlife, through national and conservation parks
Removing species that threaten human interests, such as wolves and other predators
Making humans 'plain members and citizens' of the land community, with voluntary limits on freedom
Efficient and sustainable use of natural resources, 'the greatest good for the greatest number'
questions.answerText: Efficient and sustainable use of natural resources, 'the greatest good for the greatest number'
questions.explanation: Slide 27 describes Pinchot as a conservationist (efficient, sustainable use) and enemy of the 'timber barons'; the protection-for-wildlife view is Muir's. [M1 s27, s28]

questions.stem: The following describe John Muir, except:
options: He argued for 'the greatest good for the greatest number'
He was a pioneer of conservation parks in the United States
He favoured managing natural resources primarily for protection, for the benefit of wildlife
questions.answerText: He argued for 'the greatest good for the greatest number'
questions.explanation: 'The greatest good for the greatest number' is Pinchot's utilitarian formula; Muir was non-utilitarian. [M1 s27, s28]

questions.stem: Aldo Leopold (1949) argued that we must change our relationship with nature from:
questions.explanation: Leopold's Land Ethic is a moral extension that places humans as members of the land community instead of its conquerors. [M1 s30]

questions.stem: The Land Ethic includes the following ideas, except:
options: Nature is only useful as long as it has benefits for humans
To be part of society, individuals voluntarily give up their absolute freedom
The boundaries of dependency are stretched to include nature and other living things
questions.answerText: Nature is only useful as long as it has benefits for humans
questions.explanation: Utility of nature to humans is the Dominion thesis; the Land Ethic rejects treating land as mere property. [M1 s24, s30]

questions.stem: Ecocentrism is the ethical view that:
options: Humans are the pinnacle of creation and may use nature in any way they deem beneficial, as a separate and superior entity
Humans are the primary factor in judging actions toward nature
Value is measured by the benefits that maximize societal welfare
Ecological interests must be above human-species interests when judging whether an action is right or wrong
questions.answerText: Ecological interests must be above human-species interests when judging whether an action is right or wrong
questions.explanation: This is the definition given beside Leopold's Land Ethic on slide 30. [M1 s30]

questions.stem: Which pairing of theory and core idea is correct?
options: Ecocentrism: ecological interests must be above those of the human species
Anthropocentrism: ecological interests must be above those of the human species
Utilitarianism: nature has value independently of humans
Stewardship: humans are a separate and superior entity to nature
questions.answerText: Ecocentrism: ecological interests must be above those of the human species
questions.explanation: Ecocentrism is the nature-centred end; the other pairings swap the definitions of anthropocentrism, utilitarianism, stewardship and the Dominion thesis. [M1 s24, s25, s26, s30]

questions.stem: In the conservation dilemma scenario on slide 31 (a dam threatening migratory salmon), who strongly opposed the project?
options: The energy company and the government, who expected the economic benefits
The national electricity supply authority, which feared losing power supply
Environmentalists and some members of the indigenous community
All indigenous communities, together with the government and the company
questions.answerText: Environmentalists and some members of the indigenous community
questions.explanation: The government supported the dam as it fits regional and national growth plans, while environmentalists and some indigenous members strongly opposed it. [M1 s31]

questions.stem: The dam-versus-salmon scenario resembles the Hetch Hetchy Valley dispute. Which pairing of positions is correct?
options: Pinchot: the valley must be preserved for its wildlife; Muir: dams provide the greatest good for the greatest number
Pinchot and Muir both held that nature is only useful as long as it benefits humans
Pinchot: dams give greater benefits to society; Muir: the valley is a biodiversity 'treasure' that dams disrupt
Pinchot: the dam is ethical only if it benefits the timber barons; Muir: only the government decides
Pinchot: the dam should be built to eradicate threats to the valley; Muir: the dam is acceptable if it is profitable
questions.answerText: Pinchot: dams give greater benefits to society; Muir: the valley is a biodiversity 'treasure' that dams disrupt
questions.explanation: Slide 29 contrasts Pinchot (dams give greater benefits) with Muir (Hetch Hetchy as a biodiversity treasure that dams disrupt). [M1 s29, s31]

questions.stem: In Hardin's 1968 parable of a pasture open to all, why does tragedy occur?
options: The cattle are a non-renewable resource that runs out by itself after a few seasons
The government owns the pasture and fails to tax the herdsmen who graze their cattle
Each herdsman gains privately from adding cattle while the cost of overgrazing is shared by all
The herdsmen cooperate too much and under-use the pasture
questions.answerText: Each herdsman gains privately from adding cattle while the cost of overgrazing is shared by all
questions.explanation: Each herdsman tries to keep as many cattle as possible, so the cumulative impact degrades the shared resource and no one benefits in the end. [M2 s2]

questions.stem: Which situation is the clearest example of the pattern Hardin described?
options: Overfishing in the open sea, where nobody owns the fish and nobody can be excluded
Local communities setting policy mechanisms to protect lobster fisheries
A customary forest where an indigenous community bans mining in sacred areas and protects the forest
A single owner who fences and manages his own pasture
questions.answerText: Overfishing in the open sea, where nobody owns the fish and nobody can be excluded
questions.explanation: Slide 4 lists the atmosphere and the open sea with its fish as open-access resources; slide 5's lobster fishery and customary forest are managed. [M2 s2, s4, s5]

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a commons from an open-access resource?
options: A commons has no ownership rights or possession, whereas an open-access resource is jointly owned by a defined group of users
Both exclude non-members and have joint ownership; they differ only in the size of the resource
A commons is open to the community at large with no exclusion, whereas an open-access resource excludes non-members
A commons is jointly owned by a bounded group that excludes non-members; open access has no ownership rights and no exclusion
questions.answerText: A commons is jointly owned by a bounded group that excludes non-members; open access has no ownership rights and no exclusion
questions.explanation: Slide 3's table: commons = joint ownership, narrowly defined community, non-members excluded; open access = no ownership, community at large, no exclusion. [M2 s3]

questions.stem: Fishing boats from many countries take fish from the open sea. Nobody owns the fish and nobody can be excluded. In the terms of slide 3, this resource is:
options: An open-access resource, where tragedy can occur if it is not well managed
A commons, because it is jointly owned by a restricted group
Private property with clear boundaries and a single owner who excludes everyone else
A commons whose non-members are excluded by the customary rules of the community
A resource that cannot be overused because it is renewable
questions.answerText: An open-access resource, where tragedy can occur if it is not well managed
questions.explanation: No ownership rights, the community at large and no exclusion define open access; slide 3 stresses tragedy can occur when such resources are poorly managed. [M2 s3, s4]

questions.stem: Slide 5 asks: 'Does the tragedy lie in the commons?' The lecturer's answer is that the tragedy lies in:
options: Any resource that is shared by more than one user, whether or not it has rules or monitoring
Unmanaged open access, not in the sharing of resources itself
questions.answerText: Unmanaged open access, not in the sharing of resources itself
questions.explanation: Hardin mainly described open access (no rights, rules or monitoring), not managed common property; the problem is the management regime. [M2 s5]

questions.stem: Many commons remain sustainable when they have the following, except:
options: Clear boundaries between members and non-members
Externalities that push the costs of use onto the public
Harvest rules or quotas for each user
Monitoring of compliance by officers or the community
Graduated sanctions from warnings to loss of access
questions.answerText: Externalities that push the costs of use onto the public
questions.explanation: Externalities (costs spread to the public), no institutions and high monitoring costs are what trigger tragedy, not what sustain commons. [M2 s5]

questions.stem: What is notable about the Barambang Katute customary forest?
options: An open-access forest with no rules, which has been degraded by many users
A forest owned by a mining company that restores the land after extraction
A forest managed by an indigenous community, with sacred areas where mining is not allowed
A forest managed by the central government alone, with no community role
questions.answerText: A forest managed by an indigenous community, with sacred areas where mining is not allowed
questions.explanation: Slide 5 gives it as example 2: a customary forest managed by the Barambang Katute indigenous community with protection mechanisms and mining-free sacred areas. [M2 s5]

questions.stem: What does the Barambang Katute case illustrate about Hardin's tragedy of the commons?
options: The tragedy is unavoidable whenever land is shared
Only private ownership can protect forests
Indigenous communities are exempt from state rules, so their forests cannot be overused
A defined community's own rules can protect shared resources, so the problem is unmanaged open access
questions.answerText: A defined community's own rules can protect shared resources, so the problem is unmanaged open access
questions.explanation: The case sits under the slide's question 'Does the tragedy lie in the commons?'; community mechanisms and mining bans keep the forest protected. [M2 s5]

questions.stem: How many processes does the planetary boundaries framework identify as critical for the stability and resilience of the Earth system?
questions.explanation: Slide 6: the framework identifies nine processes. (Seven of the nine were transgressed in the 2025 update.) [M2 s6, s7]

questions.stem: The planetary boundaries framework defines a scientifically based 'safe operating space for humanity' that safeguards:
options: Earth's interglacial state and its resilience
The maximum population a habitat can support
Social minimums such as food, water, health and education
Zero human impact on every Earth-system process
questions.answerText: Earth's interglacial state and its resilience
questions.explanation: Slide 6 says the framework limits the impact of the anthroposphere to safeguard the interglacial state and resilience of the Earth system. [M2 s6]

questions.stem: According to the 2025 update of the planetary boundaries (Stockholm Resilience Centre), how many of the nine boundaries have been transgressed?
questions.explanation: Slide 7: 7 out of 9 boundaries are transgressed, so Earth is outside the safe operating space. [M2 s7]

questions.stem: In the 2009 diagram only three boundaries were crossed (climate change, biodiversity loss, nitrogen cycle). Which boundary is described as newly breached in the 2025 assessment?
questions.explanation: The 2025 update adds ocean acidification to the transgressed list; only stratospheric ozone depletion and atmospheric aerosol loading stay within the safe space. [M2 s6, s7]

questions.stem: The nine planetary boundaries include the following, except:
questions.explanation: The nine are climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone depletion, atmospheric aerosol loading and novel entities. [M2 s7]

questions.stem: Excessive use of synthetic fertilisers sends too much nitrogen and phosphorus into ecosystems, causing eutrophication. Which planetary boundary does this describe?
questions.explanation: Slide 10 illustrates biogeochemical flows with fertiliser-driven N and P overflow and eutrophication, next to chemical pollution. [M2 s10]

questions.stem: According to slide 9, what has increased CO2 concentrations in the atmosphere and caused global warming and climate change?
options: Greenhouse gas emissions, particularly from burning fossil fuels
Use of hazardous chemicals such as pesticides and heavy metals that pollute the environment
questions.answerText: Greenhouse gas emissions, particularly from burning fossil fuels
questions.explanation: Slide 9 attributes climate change to GHG emissions, especially from burning fossil fuels; the other options relate to other boundaries. [M2 s8, s9, s10]

questions.stem: In the 2025 planetary boundaries diagram, climate change is assessed with which two control variables?
options: Global average temperature and sea-level rise
questions.explanation: Slide 7's diagram shows CO2 concentration and radiative forcing under climate change; genetic/functional belong to biosphere integrity, blue/green water to freshwater, N and P to biogeochemical flows. [M2 s7]

questions.stem: In Raworth's doughnut, the inner ring (the social foundation) is derived loosely from:
options: SDG-type deprivation thresholds, e.g. food, water, health, education
The nine planetary boundaries, turned inwards
The laws of ecology, such as no free lunch
The IUCN overlaps of bearable, equitable and viable
questions.answerText: SDG-type deprivation thresholds, e.g. food, water, health, education
questions.explanation: Slide 7's notes: the outer ring is the planetary boundaries model, paired with an inner ring derived loosely from SDG-type deprivation thresholds. [M2 s7]

questions.stem: Compared with planetary boundaries alone, Doughnut Economics is distinctive because it:
options: Ignores the biophysical limits of the Earth system and focuses only on social indicators of wellbeing
Replaces the nine boundaries with the 17 SDGs as its outer ring
Removes the idea of a safe operating space
Uses the boundaries as one half of a normative claim: meeting human needs without breaching them
questions.answerText: Uses the boundaries as one half of a normative claim: meeting human needs without breaching them
questions.explanation: Planetary boundaries alone are a biophysical model with no theory of wellbeing or distribution; the doughnut adds a social foundation. [M2 s7; M1 s14]

questions.stem: What is meant by the carrying capacity of an area?
options: The total number of different species that can live in a habitat at the same time
The population size at which the birth rate first exceeds the death rate in a given habitat, after which growth turns exponential
The maximum number of individuals of a species that a particular habitat can sustainably support
The fastest rate at which a population can grow when resources are unlimited
questions.answerText: The maximum number of individuals of a species that a particular habitat can sustainably support
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is the maximum number of individuals of a species a habitat can sustainably support, set by limiting factors [M3 s4]. The other options describe species richness, birth/death balance, or J-curve growth.

questions.stem: Limiting factors determine the carrying capacity of an area. Which of the following is NOT a limiting factor mentioned in the lecture?
options: Abiotic factors such as water, nutrients and climate
questions.explanation: The lecture lists space, abiotic factors and biotic factors (e.g. disease) as limiting factors; unlimited resources would give J-curve growth and are not a limit [M3 s4].

questions.stem: According to the Malthusian view of population and natural resources:
options: Population grows linearly while natural resources grow exponentially, so shortages never occur
Natural resources have fixed limits and grow arithmetically (linearly), while population tends to grow exponentially (geometrically), leading to a crisis
Both population and resources grow exponentially, so a crisis can be avoided
Technology always keeps food production ahead of population growth
Natural resources are unlimited, so population is limited only by individual choice
questions.answerText: Natural resources have fixed limits and grow arithmetically (linearly), while population tends to grow exponentially (geometrically), leading to a crisis
questions.explanation: Malthus argued resources grow arithmetically while population grows geometrically, producing a crisis period that cuts population back to what the environment can sustain [M3 s5].

questions.stem: Malthus's work is now seen as an early source of sustainability thinking, but in his time it received little attention because:
options: Population in England was shrinking rapidly at that time
He argued that natural resources are essentially unlimited, so famine could never occur in a growing population
His predictions were immediately disproved by the Green Revolution
National or global environmental issues were not yet part of political or social discourse
questions.answerText: National or global environmental issues were not yet part of political or social discourse
questions.explanation: The lecturer's notes say Malthus is regarded as the first systematic study of ecological limits to growth, yet environmental problems at national or global scale were not yet part of political or social discussion [M3 s5].

questions.stem: Overpopulation occurs when:
options: The needs of the population sustainably exceed the carrying capacity of the system
The number of people living in a region increases over time and varies across regions, as in population growth
The demand for food, water, energy, land and housing rises as population grows
The population of a country passes one billion people
questions.answerText: The needs of the population sustainably exceed the carrying capacity of the system
questions.explanation: Overpopulation is defined relative to carrying capacity [M3 s7]. A rising number of people is only population growth, and rising demand is population pressure.

questions.stem: Two regions have the same population size, but one faces much greater environmental pressure. Which explanation is consistent with the lecture on overpopulation?
options: Overpopulation is determined only by the number of people living in an area
Population growth and overpopulation are the same concept
Only the region with the faster population growth rate, regardless of consumption levels, technology or governance, can ever be considered overpopulated
The region with the larger land area never experiences population pressure
Overpopulation is not determined by population size alone but also by consumption levels, technology, resource distribution and governance
questions.answerText: Overpopulation is not determined by population size alone but also by consumption levels, technology, resource distribution and governance
questions.explanation: The lecture stresses that overpopulation depends on consumption, technology, resource distribution and governance as well as size, so equal populations need not mean equal pressure [M3 s7].

questions.stem: Barry Commoner contributed to the Neo-Malthusian debate by arguing that:
options: Population numbers have a far greater impact on the environment than technology
Technology (e.g. petrochemicals, pesticides, fossil fuels) has a greater impact on the environment than population numbers
Consumption levels have no effect on environmental damage
Food production grows exponentially while population grows linearly
questions.answerText: Technology (e.g. petrochemicals, pesticides, fossil fuels) has a greater impact on the environment than population numbers
questions.explanation: Commoner held that technology, not just population numbers, drives environmental impact [M3 s9].

questions.stem: In the Neo-Malthusian graph (population vs food production), the 'crisis point' (war, famine, etc.) occurs where:
options: The food production line falls to zero because natural resources are completely exhausted by the growing population
The J-shaped curve flattens into an S-shaped curve
The population and food production lines run parallel
The exponentially rising population curve overtakes the linearly rising food production line
questions.answerText: The exponentially rising population curve overtakes the linearly rising food production line
questions.explanation: The graph shows exponential population growth crossing linear food production, which marks the crisis point of war and famine [M3 s8].

questions.stem: What does the case study of Kerala, India show?
options: Higher GDP per capita automatically leads to higher human development, as shown by Kerala's literacy and life expectancy exceeding those of Australia and the USA
High literacy is possible only where population density is low
Kerala has the lowest literacy rate among the areas compared
High human development (literacy, life expectancy) can be achieved despite a low per-capita income
questions.answerText: High human development (literacy, life expectancy) can be achieved despite a low per-capita income
questions.explanation: Kerala has a low GDP per capita yet literacy and life expectancy comparable to developed countries, so economic capacity does not automatically raise human development [M3 s14].

questions.stem: Based on the 2022 data in the Kerala case study, Kerala's literacy rate and life expectancy were about:
questions.explanation: The table gives Kerala 94% literacy and 75 years life expectancy; 69.4/67.3 are India's, 94/68.3 are Indonesia's [M3 s14].

questions.stem: In the IPAT equation by Ehrlich & Holdren (1974), the letter A stands for:
options: Agriculture, measured by the area of farmland per person
Affluence, measured by the level of consumption or per-capita income
Adaptation, measured by the speed at which a society responds to climate change
Area, measured by the land size of a country
questions.answerText: Affluence, measured by the level of consumption or per-capita income
questions.explanation: IPAT states I = P x A x T, with A = Affluence measured by consumption level or per-capita income [M3 s17].

questions.stem: In the 2050 IPAT scenario, population rises by 35% and affluence rises about 4 times. To keep environmental quality at the 2010 level, the technology factor must reduce its impact ('decoupling') by a factor of:
questions.explanation: With P up 35% and A about 4x, impact would rise by roughly 5x, so T must fall by a factor of about five to keep I constant [M3 s19].

questions.stem: The 'dual role of technology' means that technology can:
options: Both improve environmental impact (e.g. efficiency, renewable energy) and worsen it (e.g. more exploitation, waste, increased consumption)
Act only as a technofix that eliminates every environmental problem as consumption and affluence rise, as claimed by the Kuznets-Kurzweil argument
Be used by both the Global North and the Global South
Serve as both an input and an output of the IPAT equation
questions.answerText: Both improve environmental impact (e.g. efficiency, renewable energy) and worsen it (e.g. more exploitation, waste, increased consumption)
questions.explanation: The lecture lists efficiency, renewable energy, pollution monitoring and innovation as improving impact, versus exploitation, pollution/waste and increased consumption as worsening it [M3 s21].

questions.stem: Technology can improve environmental impact in the following ways, except:
options: Efficiency in the use and management of natural resources
questions.explanation: Expansion of resource exploitation is on the 'worsening' side of the dual role; the other four are listed as improving impact [M3 s21].

questions.stem: The Jevons Paradox describes a situation in which:
options: Population grows exponentially while resources grow only arithmetically
Rising affluence and advanced technology always reduce the impact on the environment
Technological progress makes resource use more efficient, yet total consumption of the resource increases
Efficiency gains reduce resource consumption in exact proportion to the saving
questions.answerText: Technological progress makes resource use more efficient, yet total consumption of the resource increases
questions.explanation: Efficiency improves, but consumption of natural resources also rises [M3 s22]. The distractors describe Malthus, Kuznets/Kurzweil, and a naive efficiency assumption.

questions.stem: In the Jevons Paradox, a 'backfire' occurs when:
options: Excessive consumption (overconsumption) outweighs the efficiency gain, so resource use ends up higher than before
An increase in consumption merely erodes part of the efficiency benefit, while total resource use still ends up lower than before
Consumption falls as soon as efficiency improves
The savings from efficiency are reinvested in renewable energy
A new technology is abandoned because it is too expensive
questions.answerText: Excessive consumption (overconsumption) outweighs the efficiency gain, so resource use ends up higher than before
questions.explanation: The slide separates rebound (increased consumption erodes the efficiency benefit) from backfire (excessive consumption, overconsumption) [M3 s22].

questions.stem: Which statement best describes 'unequal environmental impact'?
options: Every country suffers the same share of pollution regardless of what it consumes
Environmental impacts are not always borne by those who enjoy the benefits of consumption
Countries that consume a good always pollute the most while producing it
Environmental damage occurs only in countries with large populations
Consumers and producers always share costs and benefits equally
questions.answerText: Environmental impacts are not always borne by those who enjoy the benefits of consumption
questions.explanation: Goods consumed in one country can use resources and cause pollution in another, while the benefits go to the importing country (smartphones, fast fashion, agricultural commodities) [M3 s24].

questions.stem: The lecture cites environmental and social impacts at the extraction stage of electric-vehicle battery minerals. Which pairing is given?
options: Local groundwater depletion from cobalt mining in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and child labor in Chile
Oil spills from nickel refining in China, and unsafe working conditions in Chile
Local groundwater depletion from lithium mining in Chile, and child labor in the mines of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
Deforestation from lithium mining in Indonesia, and strikes in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
questions.answerText: Local groundwater depletion from lithium mining in Chile, and child labor in the mines of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
questions.explanation: Slide 25 cites lithium mining in Chile (groundwater depletion) and DR Congo mines (unsafe conditions, child labor) as examples of environmental justice issues [M3 s25].

questions.stem: Overconsumption is best defined as:
options: Buying driven by social and psychological factors such as speed, novelty and status, with rapid turnover and many duplications, as in fast fashion
Consumption that occurs only in high-income countries
Any use of resources by a growing population
Using resources more than needed or beyond the ecosystem's ability to recover, which degrades environmental quality
questions.answerText: Using resources more than needed or beyond the ecosystem's ability to recover, which degrades environmental quality
questions.explanation: Overconsumption is excessive consumption that drives environmental damage [M3 s30, s34]. The second option is hyperconsumption.

questions.stem: Which statement about overconsumption in the Global North and Global South is correct?
options: It occurs only in the Global North because only high-income societies with industrialized economies can afford to overconsume goods and energy
It is not always tied to economic capability: the North shows consumptive lifestyles, the South resource export and rapid urbanization
It is a problem only when population exceeds the carrying capacity
It is absent in the Global South because its per-capita emissions are lower
questions.answerText: It is not always tied to economic capability: the North shows consumptive lifestyles, the South resource export and rapid urbanization
questions.explanation: Slide 33 states overconsumption is not always tied to economic capability and compares the North and South in these terms [M3 s33].

questions.stem: Hyperconsumption (Lipovetsky, 2011) refers to purchasing or using goods driven mainly by:
options: Social and psychological factors far beyond functional needs, such as speed, novelty and status
The need to meet basic survival requirements such as food, shelter and clothing at the lowest possible cost
Limited availability of goods in local markets
questions.answerText: Social and psychological factors far beyond functional needs, such as speed, novelty and status
questions.explanation: Hyperconsumption is driven by social and psychological factors, with rapid turnover and many duplications [M3 s34, s35].

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of hyperconsumption given in the lecture?
options: Buying the latest clothing styles every month (fast fashion)
Replacing gadgets every year for the latest models
Producing and buying low-priced, low-durability furniture (fast furniture)
Repairing a phone and using it for several more years
Using loan modes such as PayLater and instalments to buy more goods
questions.answerText: Repairing a phone and using it for several more years
questions.explanation: Fast fashion, fast furniture and yearly gadget replacement are the lecture's examples, with easy credit as a driver [M3 s35]; keeping a repaired phone is the opposite behaviour.

questions.stem: The ecological footprint is a measure of:
options: The amount of biologically productive land and sea area available on Earth to produce what humans demand from nature
The total volume of CO2 that a country emits from industry and transport in one calendar year
The number of people living per square kilometre
The gross domestic product generated per hectare of land
Human demand for natural capital, i.e. the amount of nature needed to support humans or an economy
questions.answerText: Human demand for natural capital, i.e. the amount of nature needed to support humans or an economy
questions.explanation: The ecological footprint tracks the land area needed to provide resources and absorb waste; the first distractor is biocapacity [M3 s37, s38].

questions.stem: The main unit used to express an individual's ecological footprint is:
options: Tonnes of CO2-equivalent per person per year
Global hectares (gha) per person per year
questions.answerText: Global hectares (gha) per person per year
questions.explanation: At the individual level the main unit is global hectares per person per year, the productive land/sea area a lifestyle requires [M3 s39].

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares ecological footprint and biocapacity?
options: Footprint is the productive land needed for what humans consume (demand); biocapacity is the productive land available (supply)
Footprint is the productive land available in nature (supply), while biocapacity is the land area needed by humans to consume (demand)
Both terms measure the same quantity, only in different units
Footprint measures only carbon emissions, while biocapacity measures only forest area
questions.answerText: Footprint is the productive land needed for what humans consume (demand); biocapacity is the productive land available (supply)
questions.explanation: The calculation compares the ecological footprint (demand) with biocapacity (supply) [M3 s38].

questions.stem: According to the Global Footprint Network figure 'Busting our Biocapacity Budget', what share of Earth's biocapacity did humanity use in 1961 and in 2020?
questions.explanation: The figure shows 73% of biocapacity used in 1961 and 160% in 2020, i.e. overshoot [M3 s38].

questions.stem: Based on the 2022 'How many Earths' data, if everyone lived like residents of the U.S.A., about how many Earths would be needed?
questions.explanation: The 2022 chart gives 5.1 Earths for the USA (5.0 in 2018), versus 0.8 for India and 1.75 for the world [M3 s41].

questions.stem: India has a far larger population than the USA, yet its lifestyle would need less than one Earth. What does this show?
options: Not only population but also how people consume determines environmental pressure
Population size is the main determinant of the ecological footprint, so more people always means more Earths
The USA has a higher biocapacity per person than India
Overpopulation is unrelated to carrying capacity
questions.answerText: Not only population but also how people consume determines environmental pressure
questions.explanation: The lecturer's note on slide 41: India's consumption can still be accommodated by <1 Earth despite its population, so consumption patterns matter as much as numbers [M3 s41].

questions.stem: According to the lecture, what share of the world's population lives in the Global South?
questions.explanation: Slide 5 lists the Global South's characteristics: less advanced economic development than the North, 88% of the world's population, larger land area, and 80% middle class by 2030 [M4 s5]. 80% is the middle-class share, not the population share.

questions.stem: Why does the lecturer stress that development decisions made in the Global South this decade are so important?
options: They will 'lock in' emissions and the global ecological footprint for decades to come
The Global South has the highest historical per-capita emissions and therefore caused most of the climate crisis
The Global North no longer has any environmental impact
The Global South has a smaller land area and population than the North
questions.answerText: They will 'lock in' emissions and the global ecological footprint for decades to come
questions.explanation: Lecturer's notes on s4-s5: Southern choices in energy, food, water and urban planning lock in the footprint and quality of life for decades, while the South has low historical per-capita emissions but is most vulnerable [M4 s4, s5].

questions.stem: The categories 'Global North' and 'Global South' are based on:
options: The hemisphere in which a country is located
Membership of the UN Security Council
Social and economic aspects, not geographical location
The latitude of the country's capital city
The size of the country's land area
questions.answerText: Social and economic aspects, not geographical location
questions.explanation: Slide 6 states the division is social and economic rather than geographic; e.g. Australia counts as Global North [M4 s6].

questions.stem: Which of the following countries is counted as part of the Global North even though it lies in the Southern Hemisphere?
questions.explanation: Australia (and New Zealand) lie in the Southern Hemisphere but are counted as Global North; Indonesia, Brazil, Chad and the Philippines are listed as Global South [M4 s6, s8].

questions.stem: On the slides, 'the commons' is defined as:
options: Natural resources that belong to no one and can be used freely by anybody without any rules or limits at all
Wealth held privately by corporations and rented to the public
Resources owned and controlled exclusively by the state
Only physical resources such as water, forest and ocean
A different kind of 'wealth' (land, culture, values, intangible heritage, etc.) owned and maintained together
questions.answerText: A different kind of 'wealth' (land, culture, values, intangible heritage, etc.) owned and maintained together
questions.explanation: Slide 11 defines the commons as a different type of wealth owned and maintained together, often tied to cultural identity and the survival of local communities [M4 s11].

questions.stem: According to the lecturer's notes, which pair of characteristics is typical of the commons, even though they still have high social value or utility?
questions.explanation: The notes say some commons are characterised by non-excludability and rivalry yet have social value/utility; this links to Hardin's tragedy of the commons [M4 s10].

questions.stem: Which of the following is a man-made commons according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: Man-made commons on slide 12 include irrigation systems, music, parks, seeds, shared knowledge, internet technology, bandwidth and libraries; forest, spectrum and biodiversity are natural commons [M4 s12].

questions.stem: The following are natural commons, except:
questions.explanation: Seeds are listed under man-made commons; air, outer space, the electromagnetic spectrum and the ocean are natural commons [M4 s12].

questions.stem: According to the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005), ecosystem services consist of:
options: Provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services
Provisioning, regulating, protecting and recreational services
Biotic, abiotic, cultural and economic services
Provisioning, trading, financial and cultural services
Regulating, mitigating, adapting and supporting services
questions.answerText: Provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services
questions.explanation: The MEA (2005) groups ecosystem services into provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural services [M4 s14].

questions.stem: Climate regulation through carbon absorption, pollination, and flood and erosion control are examples of which category of ecosystem services?
questions.explanation: Regulating services are benefits from natural regulation processes such as climate regulation, water and air purification, flood and erosion control, pollination and pest control [M4 s14].

questions.stem: In the chart of the estimated annual value of ecosystem services (Spoolman & Miller, 2021), which ecosystem has the largest value?
questions.explanation: The largest bar on slide 17 is coastal marshes/mangroves at $24.8 trillion; small in area, they provide the largest service value [M4 s17].

questions.stem: Which pairing of ecosystem and estimated annual ecosystem-service value is correct, according to the chart?
questions.explanation: Slide 17 values: forests 15.6, grasslands 12.7, cropland 9.3, swamps 1.5, mangroves 24.8, open ocean 16.3, coral reefs 9.9, marine shelf 5.9, lakes/rivers 0.9 (US$ trillion) [M4 s17].

questions.stem: Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES) is a mechanism in which:
options: Parties who benefit from nature pay those who preserve or enhance a service, provided results are achieved
Those who preserve nature pay the beneficiaries of the service to compensate them for using it, whatever the result
Local communities receive payment regardless of whether the service is delivered
All citizens are taxed equally to fund conservation in other countries
questions.answerText: Parties who benefit from nature pay those who preserve or enhance a service, provided results are achieved
questions.explanation: PES: beneficiaries (e.g. of clean water or carbon absorption) pay providers (forest farmers, coastal communities), conditional on real results [M4 s18].

questions.stem: Indigenous communities protect shared resources through customary rules and joint agreements. Which route for valuing and protecting ecosystem services does this represent?
questions.explanation: The lecture gives three routes: economic (PES), social (mutual consent as practised by indigenous communities) and governance (government regulations) [M4 s18].

questions.stem: In the Cidanau, Banten scheme (IJL, run since 2003), how much do downstream industries pay upstream farmer groups?
options: Rp12-17.5 million per hectare per year
Rp1.2-1.75 million per farmer per month
Rp1.2-1.75 million per hectare per year
Rp120-175 thousand per hectare per year
Rp1.2-1.75 billion per watershed per year
questions.answerText: Rp1.2-1.75 million per hectare per year
questions.explanation: Industries in the downstream industrial city of Cilegon pay about Rp1.2-1.75 million per hectare per year to upstream farmers to manage their gardens sustainably [M4 s18].

questions.stem: In the Cidanau watershed case, who pays whom?
options: Upstream farmers pay downstream industries for access to water
The national government pays the downstream industries to reduce their water use from the watershed
Downstream industries in Cilegon pay upstream farmers in Serang and Pandeglang
Downstream farmers pay the upstream industries for water access
questions.answerText: Downstream industries in Cilegon pay upstream farmers in Serang and Pandeglang
questions.explanation: Upstream land is managed mostly by poor farmers; downstream Cilegon industry benefits from the water service and compensates them through the FKDC scheme [M4 s18].

questions.stem: The 'hole' in the ozone layer was discovered in which year and where?
questions.explanation: In 1985 the ozone layer was found to have thinned, creating a 'hole' over Antarctica [M4 s20].

questions.stem: The ozone layer is described as a 'global commons' or 'invisible commons' because:
options: It is owned and administered by the United Nations on behalf of all member states through a global treaty body
It lies over the territory of only one country
It can be fenced and bounded like land
It cannot be seen, yet its shared benefit (blocking harmful UV radiation) is very high for everyone
It is a man-made resource created by CFC production
questions.answerText: It cannot be seen, yet its shared benefit (blocking harmful UV radiation) is very high for everyone
questions.explanation: Lecturer's notes: the ozone layer is a global/invisible commons, not visible but with high shared benefit; it blocks harmful UV radiation [M4 s20].

questions.stem: The Montreal Protocol (1987) is a global agreement that:
options: Limits NOx emissions from diesel vehicles and requires software-free emission testing in the United States
Sets the goal of limiting global warming to below 1.5 C
Prohibits the production and use of hazardous substances such as CFCs and their derivatives
Establishes jurisdictional zones such as the EEZ at sea
questions.answerText: Prohibits the production and use of hazardous substances such as CFCs and their derivatives
questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol (1987) banned CFCs and derivatives that deplete ozone [M4 s21].

questions.stem: Which pairing of agreement, year and focus is correct?
options: Montreal Protocol (2016): HFCs and other greenhouse gases only
Kigali Amendment (2016): HFC, HCFC and similar substances
Kigali Amendment (2016): NOx from diesel vehicles
questions.answerText: Kigali Amendment (2016): HFC, HCFC and similar substances
questions.explanation: Montreal Protocol (1987) targets CFCs and derivatives; the Kigali Amendment (2016) prohibits HFC, HCFC and similar substances [M4 s21].

questions.stem: According to UNESCO (cited in the lecture), around how many farmers can manage the water supply from one Subak water source?
questions.explanation: Slide 24: UNESCO notes that around 50-400 farmers can manage water from a single source [M4 s24].

questions.stem: Subak fulfils the key elements of the commons, except:
options: Shared resource: water from the same source and stream used by many farmers
Private ownership of the water by each individual farmer
Collective rules on the allocation and timing of water use
Social-cultural dimension linked to rituals, local institutions and Tri Hita Karana
questions.answerText: Private ownership of the water by each individual farmer
questions.explanation: Slide 24 lists shared resource, multiple users, collective rules, collective management and a social-cultural dimension; individual private ownership is not one of them [M4 s24].

questions.stem: In the 'Dieselgate' case, Volkswagen was proven to have:
options: Falsified diesel fuel tax records to avoid paying duties
Exported old diesel engines to the Global South
Used software that lowered NOx emissions on the road but raised them during testing so the cars looked dirtier
Exceeded CO2 limits by 20% on all vehicles sold
Used software that controlled emissions during testing, while on-road emissions increased about 20 times
questions.answerText: Used software that controlled emissions during testing, while on-road emissions increased about 20 times
questions.explanation: VW marketed its diesels as 'clean technology' but used software that controlled emissions only in testing; NOx caused smog and millions of vehicles were recalled [M4 s25].

questions.stem: What does Dieselgate illustrate about regulating a commons such as air?
options: Rules alone are not enough: industry may manipulate compliance, so monitoring and enforcement are needed
Voluntary industry self-regulation is sufficient to protect air quality, so strict government rules and testing are unnecessary
NOx limits are unnecessary because NOx is not harmful to health
Emission regulation is only relevant in the Global South
questions.answerText: Rules alone are not enough: industry may manipulate compliance, so monitoring and enforcement are needed
questions.explanation: Lecturer's notes: industry finds emission rules burdensome and may manipulate them (as VW did), so regulation needs real monitoring [M4 s25].

questions.stem: In an arrangement for managing a common resource, which element defines who may access the resource and where the management area applies?
questions.explanation: Boundaries define who has the right to access and the extent of the managed area; opportunities for use set how, when and how much to use [M4 s31].

questions.stem: A commons arrangement (Ostrom) includes the following elements, except:
options: Boundaries defining who may access the resource
Costs shared fairly among all users
Supervision of compliance with the rules
questions.explanation: The six elements are boundaries, costs, opportunities for use, supervision, sanctions and conflict resolution [M4 s31].

questions.stem: The MDGs were an international agreement adopted at the Millennium Summit in New York in September 2000. How many countries adopted them?
questions.explanation: 189 countries adopted the MDGs and 147 heads of state or government signed them at the September 2000 Millennium Summit [M5 s3].

questions.stem: Compared with the MDGs, the SDGs have a broader scope because they put stronger emphasis on:
options: Extreme poverty and hunger in developing countries only
Reducing child mortality as the single priority
Economic growth in the Global North
questions.explanation: The SDGs extend the MDGs with a stronger focus on protecting the environment and on intergenerational equity, and apply to all countries [M5 s4].

questions.stem: Sustainable development rests on the economic, social and environmental pillars. At the global scale, which two prerequisites are needed to implement it?
questions.explanation: The slide names peace and partnership (cooperation) as the two prerequisites for implementing sustainable development globally [M5 s7].

questions.stem: Globally there are 231 SDG indicators. How many indicators does Indonesia use, tailored to its national development targets?
questions.explanation: Indonesia uses 289 indicators, more than the 231 global ones, because they are adapted to national development targets [M5 s8].

questions.stem: Which institution matches and incorporates the SDG (TPB) targets and indicators into Indonesia's national development planning?
questions.explanation: Bappenas matches and incorporates the SDG targets and indicators into national development and has developed the SDG Roadmap [M5 s11].

questions.stem: To remain relevant to current conditions, the IBSAP 2025–2045 is evaluated every:
questions.explanation: One of the IBSAP functions listed on the slide is that it is evaluated every 5 years to stay relevant [M5 s19].

questions.stem: A start-up offers households a pay-per-use rental service for solar panels, using existing equipment but a new way of organising the service. In the STI definitions, this is best classified as:
options: Not STI, because innovation requires a new scientific discovery
questions.explanation: Innovation is a new way of producing, distributing or using goods and services, including new business models or new economic or social organisation [M5 s23].

questions.stem: Under the Addis Ababa Action Agenda, the creation, development and dissemination of innovations and new technologies promote sustainable development, including:
options: Compulsory transfer of all patents to developing countries
Technology transfer reserved for the Global North
Removing the private sector from the process
questions.explanation: The AAAA states that innovation and technology dissemination, including mutually agreed technology transfer, promote sustainable development [M5 s24].

questions.stem: Within the Technology Facilitation Mechanism (TFM), 2030 Connect is:
options: The annual multi-stakeholder forum on STI for the SDGs
The UN Interagency Task Team on STI for the SDGs
A group of 10 representatives supporting the TFM
A financing facility for national STI roadmaps in developing countries
An online gateway for information on STI initiatives and programmes
questions.answerText: An online gateway for information on STI initiatives and programmes
questions.explanation: 2030 Connect is the online platform; the annual STI Forum is the other communication channel, while IATT and the 10-Member Group are internal UN bodies [M5 s25].

questions.stem: Health challenges call for vaccines and diagnostics, while energy challenges call for renewables and efficiency. Which feature of STI for SDG achievement does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Goal-specific means the challenges of each SDG require different STI; place-based priority instead refers to differences between countries and regions [M5 s27].

questions.stem: In the UN midpoint assessment of 140 SDG targets (2023), what share of targets was progressing according to the roadmap?
questions.explanation: Only 15% of the 140 targets were progressing as planned; 48% were not, and more than 30% were stagnant or below the 2015 baseline [M5 s29].

questions.stem: Indonesia has taken part in the Voluntary National Review (VNR) since 2017, voluntarily, about every:
questions.explanation: Indonesia has participated actively in the VNR since 2017, roughly every 2 years, coordinated by the National TPB Secretariat [M5 s14-15].

questions.stem: Which Indonesian VNR carried the theme "Sustainable and Resilient Recovery from the COVID-19 Pandemic for the Achievement of the 2030 Agenda"?
questions.explanation: The VNR 2021 cover shows the COVID-19 recovery theme; 2017 was about eradicating poverty and 2019 about empowering people and inclusiveness [M5 s14].

questions.stem: According to the lecturer's assessment of Indonesia's TPB achievements, which statement about SDG 14 (Life below Water) and SDG 15 (Life on Land) is correct?
options: SDG 14 is declining while SDG 15 is improving
Both goals have already been fully achieved
SDG 15 is consistently declining, while SDG 14 is improving
Neither goal is covered by Indonesia's TPB reporting
questions.answerText: SDG 15 is consistently declining, while SDG 14 is improving
questions.explanation: Indonesia's SDG 15 (land ecosystems) shows a consistent decline whereas SDG 14 (marine ecosystems) is improving, which motivates stronger biodiversity commitments such as IBSAP [M5 s18].

questions.stem: In the 2023 global progress chart, roughly what share of SDG 14 and SDG 15 targets was on track?
options: About 30% of SDG 14 and 25% of SDG 15 targets
About 80% of the targets of both goals
About 15% of SDG 14 and 48% of SDG 15 targets
None of the targets of either goal
questions.answerText: About 30% of SDG 14 and 25% of SDG 15 targets
questions.explanation: In the 2023 chart the on-track share is about 30% for SDG 14 and 25% for SDG 15, with a large share stagnating or regressing [M5 s29].

questions.stem: According to the UNEP definition, Nature-based Solutions (NbS) are actions to:
options: Protect, conserve, restore, sustainably use and manage ecosystems
Replace natural ecosystems with engineered grey infrastructure wherever possible
Maximise resource extraction for short-term growth
Relocate communities away from every protected ecosystem in the country
questions.answerText: Protect, conserve, restore, sustainably use and manage ecosystems
questions.explanation: UNEP defines NbS as actions to protect, conserve, restore, sustainably use and manage ecosystems to address social, economic and environmental challenges [M5 s21].

questions.stem: The IUCN describes Nature-based Solutions as solutions that simultaneously benefit:
questions.explanation: Per IUCN, NbS deliver human well-being and biodiversity benefits at the same time, and are seen as a cost-effective way to reach the SDGs [M5 s21].

questions.stem: In the 2026 reality check ("Shared Blueprint for Peace"), electricity reaches what share of the world's population?
questions.explanation: The snapshot lists electricity reaching 92% of the world's population, internet 74% and social protection about half [M5 s30].

questions.stem: Among the areas still lagging in the 2026 reality check, global temperature by 2025 had reached how far above pre-industrial levels?
questions.explanation: By 2025 the global temperature reached 1.43°C above pre-industrial levels, close to the 1.5°C Paris limit [M5 s30].

questions.stem: Throughout Earth's history, the climate has changed due to natural factors, except:
options: Burning of fossil fuels by industry
questions.answerText: Burning of fossil fuels by industry
questions.explanation: The natural drivers named are volcanic activity, solar radiation variation, tectonic plate shifts and orbital changes; fossil-fuel burning is a human activity, which is why today's change is so fast [M6 s3].

questions.stem: Greenhouse gases (GHGs) are defined as a group of gases that:
options: Make up more than half of all air molecules near the surface
Absorb heat energy emitted from the Earth's surface
