Reflect incoming solar radiation back into space
Are produced only by industrial processes
questions.answerText: Absorb heat energy emitted from the Earth's surface
questions.explanation: GHGs absorb heat energy emitted from the Earth's surface; they are a tiny fraction (<1%) of air molecules and include natural gases as well as industrial ones [M6 s4].

questions.stem: Based on the IPCC (2021) data, what was the recorded concentration of CO₂ in 2019?
questions.explanation: The slide reports CO₂ at 409.9 ppm in 2019; 1866.3 is the CH₄ value in ppb, and 180–300 ppm was the range over the last 800,000 years [M6 s5].

questions.stem: CFCs and HCFCs are not regulated by the Kyoto Protocol. They are covered by the:
questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol regulates six GHGs (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFC, PFC, SF₆); CFCs (GWP up to ~12,500) and HCFCs fall under the Montreal Protocol [M6 s6, speaker notes].

questions.stem: According to the Cambridge Judge Business School (2024), which of the following is one of the five biggest obstacles to achieving the SDGs?
options: A growing role of the state
Reducing the scale of social enterprise
questions.explanation: The five barriers are insufficient financial resources, greenwashing by private firms, marginalisation of the state, top-down intervention, and a misguided focus on scaling social enterprise [M6 s8 notes].

questions.stem: In the discussion of SDG 13 and other SDGs, the COVID-19 pandemic is mentioned because it:
options: Reduced global GHG emissions by about 6%
questions.answerText: Reduced global GHG emissions by about 6%
questions.explanation: The slide notes that COVID-19 reduced GHG emissions by 6%, showing how closely emissions follow economic activity [M6 s9].

questions.stem: Which of the following are named as the vulnerable groups affected by climate change when SDG 13 affects other SDGs?
options: Small Island Developing States (SIDS), coastal areas, and countries in the Global South
Countries of the Global North and investors
Only people living in cold-climate regions
Landlocked high-income countries and large corporations
OECD member states and urban property owners
questions.answerText: Small Island Developing States (SIDS), coastal areas, and countries in the Global South
questions.explanation: Vulnerable groups are SIDS, coastal areas, Global South countries, and women, children, youth and other marginalized groups [M6 s9].

questions.stem: When human activities produce GHGs, roughly how much of these emissions remains in the atmosphere, while the rest is absorbed by land and oceans?
questions.explanation: About half stays in the atmosphere and the other half is absorbed by land and oceans, which is why ecosystems act as natural carbon sinks [M6 s10].

questions.stem: Restoring forests, mangroves and marine ecosystems so that they absorb carbon (carbon sequestration) is how which SDGs help to achieve SDG 13?
options: SDG 14 and SDG 15 (Life Below Water and Life on Land)
questions.answerText: SDG 14 and SDG 15 (Life Below Water and Life on Land)
questions.explanation: SDG 14 and 15 contribute through rehabilitating forests, mangroves and marine ecosystems that sequester carbon; SDG 7, 11 and 12 contribute via clean energy, green cities and waste/circular economy [M6 s10 notes].

questions.stem: Compared with the Kyoto Protocol, the Paris Agreement is different because it:
options: Asks all countries to set their own targets, known as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)
Sets top-down emission targets that only developed countries must meet
Requires only the USA to reduce its emissions
Removes any temperature limit from the agreement
questions.answerText: Asks all countries to set their own targets, known as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)
questions.explanation: Kyoto set top-down targets, excluded developing countries and was not joined by the USA; Paris asks all countries to set their own NDCs [M6 s14 notes].

questions.stem: The three goals of the Paris Agreement (2015) are:
options: Mitigation, adaptation, and making financial flows consistent with low-emission, climate-resilient development
questions.answerText: Mitigation, adaptation, and making financial flows consistent with low-emission, climate-resilient development
questions.explanation: Paris aims to limit warming well below 2°C (pursuing 1.5°C), build resilience and adaptive capacity, and align finance flows; equity/transparency/sovereignty are its principles, not goals [M6 s14, s15].

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement is implemented based on which three principles?
questions.explanation: The principles are equity (CBDR-RC), transparency (Global Stocktake) and sovereignty (bottom-up NDCs) [M6 s15].

questions.stem: The Paris principle of Sovereignty, which allows each country to determine its own level of emissions through a bottom-up architecture, is reported as:
questions.explanation: Sovereignty means bottom-up architecture: each country sets its own level of emissions and reports it as an NDC, its pledge [M6 s18].

questions.stem: The equity principle of the Paris Agreement (CBDR-RC) is associated with which negotiation terminology?
questions.explanation: Slide 16 gives 'Right to Development' as the negotiation term for the CBDR-RC principle, together with the 'ability to pay' idea [M6 s16].

questions.stem: The Global Stocktake (GST) is the representation of which principle of the Paris Agreement?
questions.explanation: GST represents the transparency principle: it assesses how far countries implement their climate commitments [M6 s17].

questions.stem: The stated objective of the Global Stocktake (GST) is to:
options: Set binding top-down emission quotas for each country
Replace all NDCs with one single global target
Punish countries that emit more than the global average
Continually increase climate ambition to avoid an emergency situation
questions.answerText: Continually increase climate ambition to avoid an emergency situation
questions.explanation: GST reviews progress and aims to continually raise climate ambition (e.g., less fossil fuel, more renewables, more climate funding) [M6 s17].

questions.stem: Indonesia ratified the Paris Agreement as Law No. 16/2016 and aims to achieve Net Zero Emission (NZE) by:
questions.explanation: Slide 19: Law No. 16/2016 ratifies Paris; Indonesia aims to limit warming to <1.5°C and reach NZE by 2060 or earlier [M6 s19].

questions.stem: In Indonesia's NDC, the 'conditional' emission reduction target is the one that:
options: Is achieved through domestic efforts alone
Is legally enforced by the United Nations
Applies only to the AFOLU sector
questions.explanation: Unconditional means independent/without intervention; conditional means achieved with international support (the higher percentage) [M6 s19-20].

questions.stem: Indonesia's Second NDC (2025) was prepared in response to the outcomes of the:
questions.explanation: The 2nd NDC explicitly responds to the outcomes of the 1st Global Stocktake (concluded at COP28, 2023) [M6 s20, s12].

questions.stem: A notable change in Indonesia's Second NDC is that its emission reduction targets are expressed as:
options: Relative to a business-as-usual baseline only
questions.explanation: The SNDC shifts to absolute emission targets (31.89% unconditional, 43.20% conditional by 2035), a more modern methodology aligned with UNFCCC transparency standards [M6 s20 notes].

questions.stem: Hot weather occurs throughout cities, but the effects of urban heat may differ based on:
options: The number of cities in the country
The total volume of carbon sequestration
questions.explanation: Slide 26 says the heat affects the whole city but impacts vary by socio-economic status, an equity dimension of urban heat [M6 s26].

questions.stem: Because AC use can raise energy consumption and refrigerant (HFC) emissions, relying on AC as a climate adaptation strategy creates a potential for:
questions.explanation: AC saves lives but increases GHG emissions, so it can be a maladaptation, which is why sustainable cooling is needed [M6 s27].

questions.stem: A technician releases old refrigerant into the air while servicing an AC unit. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Direct emissions come from refrigerant leakage and unsustainable refrigerant handling during servicing; indirect emissions come from the energy used [M6 s28].

questions.stem: Which of the following is not one of the principles of sustainable cooling presented in the lecture?
options: Banning all cooling in tropical cities
questions.answerText: Banning all cooling in tropical cities
questions.explanation: The principles are energy savings, environmentally friendly refrigerants, renewable energy integration, fair and affordable access, and circular economy/end-of-life management [M6 s29].

questions.stem: Which example illustrates the 'fair and affordable access' principle of sustainable cooling?
options: Reducing the thermal load with shading
Cold storage for traditional fishermen and village cooperatives in need
questions.answerText: Cold storage for traditional fishermen and village cooperatives in need
questions.explanation: Slide 29 gives cold storage for traditional fishermen and village cooperatives as the fair-access example [M6 s29].

questions.stem: In 2019, which sector contributed 22% (13 GtCO₂-eq) of global GHG emissions?
options: AFOLU (Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use)
questions.answerText: AFOLU (Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use)
questions.explanation: 2019 shares: Energy 34%, Industry 24%, AFOLU 22%, Transportation 15%, Building 6% [M6 s32].

questions.stem: CO₂ captured from industrial sources (such as steel or cement production) or power plants and injected into porous rock underground for long-term storage is an example of:
questions.explanation: Geological sequestration stores CO₂ from industrial/energy sources in underground rock formations; biological uses vegetation, soil and oceans [M6 s33 notes].

questions.stem: Tropical peatlands and other peatlands cover only about 3% of the world's land. How does the carbon they store compare with all forests?
questions.explanation: Peatlands cover about 3% of land but store twice as much carbon as all forests, so protecting and restoring them matters for climate [M6 s10 notes].

questions.stem: In tropical peatlands, the most important factor regulating peat decomposition is:
options: The depth of the mineral subsoil
A high water table level that limits oxygen availability
The type of crops planted nearby
questions.answerText: A high water table level that limits oxygen availability
questions.explanation: A high water table keeps the peat waterlogged and limits oxygen for aerobic decomposers, so plant litter accumulates as peat [M6 s35 notes].

questions.stem: By 2010, what share of the 55.81 Mha of Borneo forests recorded in 1973 had been logged over?
questions.explanation: Gaveau et al. (2014): 26.63 Mha (47.72%) of Borneo's forest had been logged by 2010, part of Indonesia's rapid peatland degradation [M6 s36].

questions.stem: In tropical peatlands in Indonesia, the 'cold fire' is:
options: An extensive fire that occurs occasionally in dry El Niño years
The release of methane from rice paddies
The storage of carbon in permanently waterlogged anoxic peat
A steady CO₂ emission from aerobic decomposition after drainage lowers the water table
questions.answerText: A steady CO₂ emission from aerobic decomposition after drainage lowers the water table
questions.explanation: Drainage makes the upper peat aerobic so microbes decompose it continuously (steady emission), unlike occasional but extensive dry-season fires [M6 s36 notes].

questions.stem: Among AFOLU mitigation strategies, reforestation refers to:
options: Restoring forest cover on land that recently lost its forest due to fire, logging or conversion
Planting trees together with crops or livestock on the same land
Using crop residues as a source of bioenergy
Establishing a new forest on land that was not forest
questions.answerText: Restoring forest cover on land that recently lost its forest due to fire, logging or conversion
questions.explanation: Reforestation restores forest on recently deforested land; afforestation plants forest on non-forest land; agroforestry mixes trees with crops/livestock [M6 s38 notes].

questions.stem: Which of the following is a human-made (industrial) greenhouse gas?
questions.explanation: Industrial GHGs include CFCs, HFCs, PFCs and SF₆; N₂, O₂ and NH₃ are not GHGs, and water vapor is a natural GHG [M6 s4].

questions.stem: Besides passive design, which measure belongs to the 'energy savings' principle of sustainable cooling?
options: Using energy-efficient ACs, refrigerators, freezers, cold storage and chillers
questions.answerText: Using energy-efficient ACs, refrigerators, freezers, cold storage and chillers
questions.explanation: Energy savings means energy-efficient equipment plus passive design (ventilation, insulation, shading); the other options belong to other principles [M6 s29].

questions.stem: In the principle of environmentally friendly refrigerants, the requirement of 'low GWP' is meant so that the refrigerant does not:
options: Increase the thermal load of buildings
questions.explanation: Zero ODP protects the ozone layer, while low GWP means the refrigerant does not contribute to global warming [M6 s29].

questions.stem: Integrating renewable energy into cooling systems mainly helps to reduce which type of emissions?
options: Indirect emissions from the energy consumed by cooling
questions.answerText: Indirect emissions from the energy consumed by cooling
questions.explanation: Indirect emissions come from energy consumption of cooling (50-60% of a commercial building's energy), so powering it with renewables such as solar cuts them [M6 s28, s29].

questions.stem: A workshop collects old refrigerant from retired AC units instead of venting it and sends the units for recycling. Which principle of sustainable cooling does this follow?
questions.explanation: Managing used refrigerants (not releasing them directly into the air) and recycling cooling units is the circular economy and end-of-life principle [M6 s29].

questions.stem: Large-scale agricultural expansion in rural areas (SDG 2) is a mixed activity. The following are negative impacts it can cause, except
options: Being among the largest users of freshwater (SDG 6)
Chemical use and land degradation (SDG 12 and 15)
questions.explanation: Agricultural expansion improves nutrition but drives deforestation, uses most freshwater, and can lower local quality of life and widen inequality, not narrow it [M7 s8].

questions.stem: In the inverted-U curve linking per capita income to per capita material footprint, what happens after the turning point?
options: The per capita material footprint starts to fall
The per capita material footprint keeps rising with income
Per capita income falls back to zero
The footprint stays fixed at its maximum value
questions.answerText: The per capita material footprint starts to fall
questions.explanation: The curve rises to a turning point and then declines, so technology and affluence first raise the footprint and only later may decouple it [M7 s15].

questions.stem: In the nexus approach, how should a country prioritise the SDGs?
options: In the same order as the global SDG ranking
By following the priorities of the Global North
By choosing only the environmental goals
questions.explanation: The nexus slide states that the country prioritises SDGs depending on the local context, so there is no one-size-fits-all [M7 s21].

questions.stem: In the SDG wheel of the Food–Energy–Water nexus, which three SDGs form the inner ring (food, water and energy security)?
questions.explanation: The inner ring holds SDG 2 (food security), SDG 6 (water security) and SDG 7 (energy security); other SDGs sit in the middle and outer rings [M7 s22].

questions.stem: Under the "Security" reason for the FEW nexus approach, the absence or crisis of any one of food, energy or water results in:
options: No effect on the other two sectors
An automatic increase in SDG funding
A temporary fall in all resource prices worldwide
questions.explanation: Food, energy and water are fundamental for society, so a crisis in any one of them causes social instability and economic disruption [M7 s25].

questions.stem: An SDG spillover refers to:
options: The transfer of SDG funds from the Global North to the Global South to close financing gaps
Two SDGs reinforcing each other within one country's policy mix
The effect of one country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG progress
The overflow of surplus indicators into national reports
questions.answerText: The effect of one country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG progress
questions.explanation: A spillover is the influence of one country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG achievement, even while its own ranking improves [M7 s5].

questions.stem: Indonesia imports rice to meet its food needs (target 2.1). Which cross-border effect may this cause, as an example of an SDG trade-off?
options: Loss of biodiversity in the exporting country (target 15.5)
Reduced hunger in the exporting country thanks to a larger rice supply (target 2.1)
A synergy that needs no further attention
A lower material footprint in the exporting country
questions.answerText: Loss of biodiversity in the exporting country (target 15.5)
questions.explanation: Importing food can cause biodiversity loss in the exporter (target 15.5), an SDG trade-off across borders [M7 s5].

questions.stem: The 2030 Agenda says SDGs are not achieved one by one but rest on the following principles, except
questions.explanation: The M7 mandate is transformative, universal and indivisible; place-based priority is a feature of STI from M5, not of this mandate [M7 s6].

questions.stem: Why can traditional analysis of SDG achievement, such as country rankings or linear correlations, be misleading?
options: It covers too few countries to be statistically valid for comparison
It includes only the environmental dimension of sustainability
It always ranks Global South countries above Global North countries
It is prohibited under the 2030 Agenda and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda
It ignores interlinkages, local context, "No One Left Behind" and spillovers
questions.answerText: It ignores interlinkages, local context, "No One Left Behind" and spillovers
questions.explanation: Rankings and linear correlations oversimplify complex, interlinked goals and miss local context, No One Left Behind and spillover effects [M7 s6].

questions.stem: In the two-objective grid of SDG interlinkages, a positive change in Objective A that comes with a negative change in Objective B is called a:
questions.explanation: A trade-off is counteracting: progress on one goal delays another. A synergy has positive change in both objectives [M7 s6, s8].

questions.stem: Which policy direction follows from the idea of synergies and trade-offs among SDGs?
options: Pursue each SDG separately to avoid interference
Scale up synergies and manage or decouple trade-offs
Drop any SDG that causes a trade-off
Ignore trade-offs because they cancel out in the long run
questions.answerText: Scale up synergies and manage or decouple trade-offs
questions.explanation: Synergies accelerate SDG achievement and trade-offs need special attention, so the aim is to maximise synergies and minimise trade-offs [M7 s6].

questions.stem: In the activity classification, what is the strategic imperative for opposed activities such as coal mining or alcohol and cigarette production?
options: Explore ways to add positive impact
Transform themselves to align with the SDG agenda
Keep current practice because their effects are insignificant
questions.answerText: Transform themselves to align with the SDG agenda
questions.explanation: Opposed activities mainly harm the SDGs, so they must transform; core activities scale, mixed ones decouple, peripheral ones explore [M7 s9].

questions.stem: Education, public health, legal activities and scientific research are examples of which type of activity, whose strategy is to increase positive impact?
questions.explanation: Core activities generate many positive and few negative impacts, and their strategy is to scale the positive impact [M7 s7].

questions.stem: Since 2018, China no longer accepts imported recyclables below which purity level?
questions.explanation: Recycling can cost more than new material, and China has rejected recyclables below 99% purity since 2018 [M7 s11].

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts single stream and dual stream recycling?
options: Single stream sorts by material quality at source, while dual stream mixes all materials together
Both systems give the same market value but differ only in collection cost
Single stream mixes material qualities in one container; dual stream sorts by quality and raises value
Dual stream is convenient for households but mixes and contaminates materials
questions.answerText: Single stream mixes material qualities in one container; dual stream sorts by quality and raises value
questions.explanation: Single stream is convenient but mixes qualities; dual stream sorts by quality and raises value, showing the convenience versus cost/quality trade-off [M7 s11].

questions.stem: Based on Boar et al. (2021), synergy among SDGs in the Global North includes:
options: Only one dimension, as in the Global South
Only the economic dimension of growth and trade
All three dimensions (social, economic and environmental)
None; the Global North has only trade-offs among SDGs
questions.answerText: All three dimensions (social, economic and environmental)
questions.explanation: Boar et al. found Global North synergies span social, economic and environmental dimensions, while Global South synergies cover only one [M7 s17].

questions.stem: According to Boar et al. (2021), which factor reduces the impact on the environmental dimension in the Global North's SDG synergies?
questions.explanation: The slide notes that new technology and renewable energy reduce environmental-dimension impacts in the Global North [M7 s17].

flashcards.front: What is an ecosystem, and how large can it be?
flashcards.back: A functional unit of a community of living organisms (biotic) and their environment (abiotic), linked by energy flow and nutrient cycling. Can be a lake, forest or island, or the space under a fallen log; the biosphere is the global ecosystem. Any activity in one affects its material cycles and energy flows [M1 s15-16].

flashcards.front: Who was John Muir and what was his position on nature?
flashcards.back: Naturalist and Sierra Club founder; a preservationist and non-utilitarian: nature should be managed primarily for protection, for the benefit of wildlife rather than human consumption. Pioneer of US conservation parks (Yosemite). Opposed the Hetch Hetchy dam, a step toward non-anthropocentric ethics [M1 s28-29].

flashcards.front: Summarise the Hetch Hetchy dispute: who argued what?
flashcards.back: Dam in Yosemite to supply water to San Francisco (approved 1913). Pinchot (conservationist, utilitarian): the dam brings greater benefits to society. Muir (preservationist, non-utilitarian): the valley is a biodiversity treasure and the dam disrupts wildlife [M1 s29].

flashcards.front: What are open-access resources? Give examples.
flashcards.back: Renewable resources not owned by anyone and usable by almost anyone. Fully open: the atmosphere and the open sea and its fish. Often used collectively but not entirely open: grasslands, forests, rivers, aquifers. Most at risk of a Hardin-style tragedy; global ones need collective agreements [M2 s4].

flashcards.front: Planetary boundary: land-system change - what drives it and what is its 2025 status?
flashcards.back: Large-scale land conversion for agriculture, urbanisation and deforestation disrupts ecosystems, reduces biodiversity and alters carbon and water cycles. Control variable: remaining forest cover. Status 2025: transgressed [M2 s7-8].

flashcards.front: Planetary boundary: biogeochemical flows - cause, effect, status?
flashcards.back: Excess synthetic fertiliser sends nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) into ecosystems, causing eutrophication (algal blooms, oxygen depletion, dead zones) and disrupting nutrient cycles. Status 2025: transgressed, with N and P deep in the high-risk zone [M2 s6, s7, s10].

flashcards.front: IPAT 2050 scenario: what must happen to technology to keep impact constant?
flashcards.back: Base 2010: population +35% (x1.35), affluence about x4. With T constant, I = 1.35 x 4 = 5.4 times today. To keep I constant, technology must decouple: cut impact per unit of consumption by a factor of about five (Factor Five) [M3 s19].

flashcards.front: Give everyday examples of overconsumption and of planned obsolescence.
flashcards.back: Overconsumption: AC very cold all day, lights left on, oversized portions and food waste, single-use plastic, excess fertiliser. Planned obsolescence: products designed with a limited life, e.g. incandescent bulbs limited to about 1,000 hours (Phoebus cartel), DuPont nylon stockings, electronics, furniture [M3 s33].

flashcards.front: How is an individual's ecological footprint measured?
flashcards.back: Unit: global hectare (gha) per person per year (a hectare of world-average productivity). Components: food consumption, energy and materials for the home, mobility, and waste. Tools: Footprint Calculator (how many Earths if everyone lived this way) and the Global Footprint Network data portal [M3 s39, s42].

flashcards.front: Which four calculation types does Week 3 test, and what is each formula?
flashcards.back: 1) IPAT: required T reduction = P multiplier x A multiplier. 2) Density difference = density A - density B. 3) Electricity cost = kW x h/day x days x price per kWh. 4) Footprint: balance = biocapacity - footprint; Earths = footprint / biocapacity. Always convert W to kW and % to a multiplier first [M3 s14-41].

flashcards.front: IPAT decoupling: how do you compute the required reduction in T?
flashcards.back: Hold I constant: required T reduction = P multiplier x A multiplier, where +35% = x1.35. Multiply, do not add. Example: P +35%, A x4 gives 1.35 x 4 = 5.4, about factor five. P +20%, A x2.5 gives 1.2 x 2.5 = 3 [M3 s17, s19].

flashcards.front: How do you compute a population-density difference? Quiz example?
flashcards.back: Difference = density(A) - density(B), using the 2022 data (persons per km2): Kerala 860, India 488, Australia 3.5, Germany 242, USA 37.8, Indonesia 141. Example: Kerala - Indonesia = 860 - 141 = 719 per km2. Traps: 488 and 141 are single densities [M3 s14].

flashcards.front: Formula for the electricity cost of an appliance? Worked example?
flashcards.back: Cost = kW x hours/day x days x price per kWh; convert W to kW first (/1,000). Example: 20 bulbs x 15 W = 300 W = 0.3 kW; 0.3 x 10 h x 30 d x Rp1,000 = Rp90,000. AC 750 W: 0.75 x 12 x 30 x Rp1,500 = Rp405,000 [M3 s22, s33].

flashcards.front: How do you calculate overshoot and 'how many Earths'?
flashcards.back: Balance = biocapacity - footprint (negative = deficit). Overshoot ratio = footprint / biocapacity; Earths = percentage / 100. Example: Indonesia 1.2 - 1.8 = -0.6 gha (footprint 150% of biocapacity); humanity 160% in 2020 = 1.6 Earths. Unit: gha per person per year [M3 s38, s40, s41].

flashcards.front: Give the key data on the Global South.
flashcards.back: Economic development less advanced than the Global North; about 88% of the world's population; a larger land area; expected to host about 80% of the global middle class by 2030, so consumption (A in IPAT) will grow fastest there [M4 s5].

flashcards.front: Why are commons in the Global South culturally important, and what threatens them?
flashcards.back: Commons are tied to cultural identity, spirituality and survival of indigenous and local communities; a forest is a pharmacy, a spiritual place and guardian of the water cycle, and traditional knowledge is an intellectual commons. Threats: corporate exploitation, policies excluding local communities, climate change [M4 s11].

flashcards.front: What are cultural ecosystem services? Give examples.
flashcards.back: Non-material benefits for spiritual, cognitive and recreational development: aesthetic value and recreation (nature tourism), spiritual and religious value of sacred places, inspiration for education, art and culture, and cultural heritage and identity. Example: Subak water temples and Tri Hita Karana [M4 s14].

flashcards.front: How does technological progress affect the management of commons?
flashcards.back: It can cause exclusion or reduced joint access, or strengthen collective capacity. Listed technologies: fences/stakes, information and data, energy, time-saving automation, (intellectual) property rights. Without clear goals and regulation protecting shared value, technology tends to privatise and fragment commons [M4 s32].

flashcards.front: Why do cross-cutting themes matter, and which five does the course use?
flashcards.back: They connect concepts from different weeks, so they suit essay and comparison questions. Themes: **Technology** (problem or solution?), **Equity** (Global North vs South), **Commons** and their governance, **Limits** of the planet, and **SDGs as a connected system**.

flashcards.front: Technology: how can it raise or cut impact? Name concepts from several weeks.
flashcards.back: Dual role. W3: IPAT's T, Jevons paradox (rebound/backfire), Neo-Malthusian technology (Commoner). W4: technology can privatise commons. W5: STI, TFM. W6: CCUS, AC (adaptation vs emissions). W7: technology raises material footprint (SDG 12), Responsible Innovation.

flashcards.front: Equity: who causes, suffers and pays for impacts? List linked concepts.
flashcards.back: W3 environmental justice and consumption inequality (richest 10% ~ half of CO2, poorest 50% ~10%); W4 Global North/South is socio-economic; W5 equity discussion; W6 CBDR-RC (developed countries commit more); W7 cross-border spillovers and Boar et al. (North synergies span 3 dimensions, South only 1).

flashcards.front: How do the commons weeks connect (Hardin, Ostrom, Montreal, Subak, PES, Paris)?
flashcards.back: W2 Hardin: tragedy comes from unmanaged open access. W4: commons arrangements (boundaries, costs, rules, supervision, graduated sanctions, conflict resolution), Montreal Protocol (1987)/Kigali (2016), Subak, payment for ecosystem services. W6: the Paris Agreement regulates the atmosphere as a global commons via NDCs.

flashcards.front: What concepts make up the theme 'Limits of the planet' and what numbers matter?
flashcards.back: Carrying capacity and Malthus (W3); ecological footprint vs biocapacity (73% in 1961, 160% in 2020); planetary boundaries (9 processes; 7 of 9 transgressed in 2025); Doughnut Economics and laws of ecology (W1); GHGs (W6). Overshoot = footprint above biocapacity or beyond the ecological ceiling.

flashcards.front: How do the SDGs work as a connected system (W1, W5, W6, W7)?
flashcards.back: W5: 17 goals, 169 targets, 231 global indicators, inseparable whole (2015-2030). W1: three dimensions. W6: SDG 13 affects other SDGs and vice versa. W7: interlinkages (maximise synergies, minimise trade-offs; transformative, universal, indivisible) and the FEW nexus (SDG 2, 6, 7 at the centre).

flashcards.front: Why is sustainability called an 'open-ended, positive and temporary' concept?
flashcards.back: Slide 11: no single scientific definition fixes it. It is **open-ended** because the social understanding of sustainable development depends on time and situation, culture and knowledge. Hopwood et al. (2005) map views from status quo (World Bank, OECD) through reform to transformation (deep ecology, indigenous/Global South movements).

flashcards.front: List the milestones in the history of the sustainability idea (slide 12).
flashcards.back: 1713 Carlowitz (sustainable forest use); Malthus (limits to growth, famine/epidemics/war); 1960s Boulding, Ayres & Kneese, Georgescu-Roegen, Daly (nature back on the economic agenda); Brundtland Commission (WCED) *Our Common Future*; 1994 German Advisory Council (3 responsibilities); 2003 unidimensional vs multidimensional concepts.

flashcards.front: State the Brundtland definition of sustainable development and its source.
flashcards.back: From the WCED report *Our Common Future*: development that **meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs**. The report stresses that environment, economy and society are interdependent and interconnected.

flashcards.front: Name the three dimensions of sustainability and the IUCN Venn overlaps.
flashcards.back: **Economic**, **Environmental**, **Social**. Overlaps: Social ∩ Environment = Bearable; Social ∩ Economic = Equitable; Environment ∩ Economic = Viable; all three = Sustainable. Slide 15: the environment is foundational; society and economy must operate within planetary boundaries.

flashcards.front: What is Doughnut Economics (Raworth) and what do its two rings represent?
flashcards.back: A safe and just space for humanity. **Outer ring** = ecological ceiling (planetary boundaries; beyond it = overshoot). **Inner ring** = social foundation (water, food, health, education, etc.; below it = shortfall). The doughnut between them is the aim: meeting everyone's needs within environmental limits.

flashcards.front: List the six laws of ecology.
flashcards.back: 1) Every element is connected to everything else. 2) Every species depends on every other species. 3) Everything must go somewhere. 4) The laws of thermodynamics apply. 5) Nature knows best. 6) There is no such thing as a free lunch.

flashcards.front: Define the Dominion thesis and give its historical illustration.
flashcards.back: Humans are the pinnacle of creation, a separate and superior entity to nature, with the ethical freedom to use it in any way they deem beneficial; nature is only useful as long as it benefits humans. Illustration: the 17th-century wolf eradication programme, among the first environmental regulations in North America.

flashcards.front: Define anthropocentrism and name its opposite.
flashcards.back: Anthropocentrism: the ethical viewpoint that **humans are the primary factor** in determining whether actions toward nature are right or wrong. Its opposite is **ecocentrism** (ecological interests above human interests). Slide 22 example: water pollution harming human health downstream is an anthropocentric argument.

flashcards.front: Compare Pinchot (conservation) and Muir (preservation).
flashcards.back: **Pinchot**: conservationist; efficient and sustainable use of natural resources, 'the greatest good for the greatest number'; enemy of the timber barons. **Muir**: preservationist; protection of nature for the benefit of wildlife; non-utilitarian; pioneer of conservation parks in the US. They clashed over the Hetch Hetchy dam.

flashcards.front: What is Leopold's Land Ethic?
flashcards.back: Aldo Leopold (1949): land is not just 'property'. Individuals voluntarily give up absolute freedom to belong to a community, and the community is stretched to include nature and other living things. A moral extension: from 'conqueror' to 'plain member and citizen'. It leads to ecocentrism.

flashcards.front: Define ecocentrism.
flashcards.back: The view that **ecological interests must be above the interests of the human species** in determining whether an action is right or wrong. It sits at the nature-centred end of the ethics spectrum, opposite to anthropocentrism, and follows from Leopold's Land Ethic.

flashcards.front: Summarise the conservation dilemma scenario (dam vs salmon) and who takes which side.
flashcards.back: An energy company's dam brings electricity, employment and economic benefits, but blocks migratory salmon routes and threatens indigenous people whose livelihoods depend on salmon. The government supports it; environmentalists and some indigenous members strongly oppose it. Answer by weighing stakeholders, ethical theories and trade-offs.

flashcards.front: Explain Hardin's tragedy of the commons (1968).
flashcards.back: Garrett Hardin, *Science* 1968: on a pasture open to all each herdsman keeps as many cattle as possible. Benefits are private, costs are shared. Each thinks his little use does not matter, but the cumulative impact degrades or destroys the resource: no one benefits, everyone loses.

flashcards.front: Compare a commons with an open-access resource.
flashcards.back: **Commons**: joint ownership; a narrowly defined group with clear boundaries; non-members excluded. **Open access**: no ownership rights or possession; the community at large; no exclusion (e.g. atmosphere, open sea and its fish). Tragedy can occur in open-access resources that are not well managed.

flashcards.front: Does the tragedy lie in the commons? Why or why not?
flashcards.back: No: the tragedy lies in **unmanaged open access** (no rights, rules or monitoring). Many commons stay sustainable with clear boundaries, harvest rules/quotas, monitoring, graduated sanctions and dispute forums. Triggers of tragedy: no institutions, high monitoring costs, externalities, scale mismatch (e.g. atmosphere). Problem = management regime.

flashcards.front: What is the Barambang Katute customary forest an example of?
flashcards.back: An example on slide 5 that commons can be protected: the customary (adat) forest is managed by the Barambang Katute indigenous community, which has protection mechanisms and sacred areas where mining is not allowed. Shows the problem is unmanaged open access, not shared ownership.

flashcards.front: What is the planetary boundaries framework?
flashcards.back: Earth-system-science framework (Rockström et al. 2009) identifying **nine processes** critical for Earth-system stability and resilience. It sets limits on human (anthroposphere) impact, defining a scientifically based **safe operating space for humanity** that safeguards Earth's interglacial state and its resilience.

flashcards.front: What is the 2025 status of the planetary boundaries?
flashcards.back: **7 of 9 transgressed** (Stockholm Resilience Centre, Sept 2025): climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows, novel entities and ocean acidification (newly breached). Still safe: stratospheric ozone depletion and atmospheric aerosol loading. In 2009 only 3 were crossed.

flashcards.front: List the nine planetary boundaries grouped by 2025 status.
flashcards.back: **Transgressed (7)**: climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows (N, P), novel entities, ocean acidification. **Within safe space (2)**: stratospheric ozone depletion, atmospheric aerosol loading. The boundaries are interlinked (e.g. deforestation affects climate, biodiversity and rainfall).

flashcards.front: Why is climate change a planetary boundary issue, and which variables show it is transgressed?
flashcards.back: GHG emissions, especially from burning fossil fuels, raise atmospheric CO2 and cause global warming. The 2025 diagram shows both control variables, **CO2 concentration** and **radiative forcing**, beyond the boundary. Climate interacts with most other boundaries; Week 6 covers Paris, CBDR-RC and NDCs.

flashcards.front: How do planetary boundaries relate to Doughnut Economics?
flashcards.back: Raworth's doughnut is built on planetary boundaries: the **outer ring** is the boundaries repurposed as an ecological ceiling; the **inner ring** is a social foundation derived loosely from SDG-type deprivation thresholds. The space between is the safe and just space. Boundaries alone = biophysical; doughnut adds a normative claim.

flashcards.front: Define carrying capacity and name what sets it.
flashcards.back: Maximum number of individuals of a species a habitat can sustainably support. Set by limiting factors: space, abiotic factors (water, nutrients, climate) and biotic factors (e.g. disease). Growth is a J-curve far below K and becomes an S-curve (logistic) as it nears K.

flashcards.front: State Malthus's argument about population and resources.
flashcards.back: Resources have fixed limits and grow arithmetically (linearly); population grows exponentially (geometrically). The gap leads to a crisis period (famine, disease, war) that pushes population back to a sustainable level. Seen as the first systematic study of ecological limits to growth.

flashcards.front: When does population growth become overpopulation?
flashcards.back: When the needs of the population sustainably exceed the carrying capacity of the system. Not determined by size alone: consumption levels, technology, resource distribution and governance matter. Population growth = demographic fact; population pressure = rising demand; overpopulation = demand beyond capacity.

flashcards.front: Compare the Neo-Malthusian view with Malthus; what did Commoner add?
flashcards.back: Neo-Malthusians apply Malthus to modern problems: social, economic and environmental interactions cause scarcity and damage; they propose population control and efficient resource use. Barry Commoner: technology (petrochemicals, pesticides, fossil fuels) impacts the environment more than population numbers.

flashcards.front: What does Kerala (India) show about income and human development?
flashcards.back: High human development does not require high income. 2022: Kerala GDP per capita about US$3,100, literacy 94%, life expectancy 75 years, density 860/km2, comparable to developed countries and above India's average (69.4%, 67.3 yr). Economic capacity alone does not raise human development.

flashcards.front: Write the IPAT equation and explain each term.
flashcards.back: I = P x A x T (Ehrlich & Holdren, 1974). I = environmental impact, P = population, A = affluence (consumption level or per-capita income), T = technology (impact per unit of consumption). 2050 case: P +35%, A about 4x means T must fall by a factor of about 5.

flashcards.front: Explain the dual role of technology.
flashcards.back: Improves impact: efficiency in resource use and management, renewable energy, pollution monitoring, innovation. Worsens impact: expansion of natural resource exploitation, pollution and waste, increased consumption. Example: coal raises GHG emissions, solar reduces them, yet coal replacing firewood can reduce deforestation.

flashcards.front: What is the Jevons Paradox? Distinguish rebound and backfire.
flashcards.back: Technological progress makes resource use more efficient but also increases total consumption. Rebound: increased consumption eats into the efficiency gain. Backfire: excessive consumption (overconsumption) outweighs the gain, so use ends up higher than before.

flashcards.front: Why is environmental impact 'unequal'? Give examples.
flashcards.back: Impacts are not always borne by those who enjoy the benefits. Smartphones (minerals mined elsewhere), fast fashion (water, energy, waste in producing region), agricultural commodities (land-use change in producers). Offshoring since the 1970s; EV minerals (Chile lithium groundwater, DR Congo child labor); AI data centres.

flashcards.front: Define overconsumption and list the perspectives on consumption.
flashcards.back: Using resources more than needed or beyond the ecosystem's ability to recover, degrading environmental quality. Perspectives: rational, cultural, pleasurable, identity, communication. Not always tied to economic capability: North = consumptive lifestyle and high industrialization; South = resource export and rapid urbanization.

flashcards.front: Compare hyperconsumption with overconsumption.
flashcards.back: Hyperconsumption (Lipovetsky, 2011): buying driven by social and psychological factors (speed, novelty, status) far beyond functional needs, with rapid turnover and duplication; drivers include trends, technology and loans (PayLater, instalments). Overconsumption: use beyond need or ecosystem recovery. Examples: fast fashion, fast furniture, yearly gadgets.

flashcards.front: Define the ecological footprint and its unit.
flashcards.back: A measure of human demand for natural capital: the land area needed to provide resources and absorb waste, so a measure of human impact. More consumption means a larger footprint. Individual unit: global hectares (gha) per person per year (food, home energy and materials, mobility, waste).

flashcards.front: Footprint vs biocapacity: what is compared and what are the key numbers?
flashcards.back: Footprint = productive land needed for all human consumption (demand); biocapacity = productive land available (supply). Footprint above biocapacity = overshoot. Global Footprint Network: humanity used 73% of biocapacity in 1961 and 160% in 2020.

flashcards.front: What do the 'How many Earths' figures show, with key numbers?
flashcards.back: Earths needed if everyone lived like a given country (2022): USA 5.1, Australia 4.5, Russia 3.4, Germany 3.0, China 2.4, Brazil 1.6, India 0.8, World 1.75. India has far more people than the USA but needs <1 Earth: how people consume matters, not only how many.

flashcards.front: Why does the Global South matter for sustainability? Give key facts.
flashcards.back: Characteristics: less advanced economic development, 88% of world population, larger land area, 80% middle class by 2030. Most future population growth and urbanisation; holds tropical forests and biodiversity; low historical per-capita emissions yet most vulnerable. Decisions now lock in emissions for decades; justice is central.

flashcards.front: How are Global North and Global South defined? Give exceptions.
flashcards.back: Based on social and economic aspects, not geographical location. North: high income, strong industry/tech, dominates institutions, most historical emissions. South: middle/low income, vulnerable, South-South cooperation. Exceptions: Australia and New Zealand (south but North); Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong in IMF advanced list.

flashcards.front: What does 'the commons' mean?
flashcards.back: A different kind of wealth (land, culture, values, activities, intangible heritage) owned and maintained together; tied to cultural identity and community survival. Notes: Hardt & Negri (2009); non-excludability and rivalry yet high social value; a system of resource, users, rules and institutions; not binary property vs none.

flashcards.front: List natural vs man-made commons.
flashcards.back: Natural: water, air, land, forest, ocean, biodiversity, electromagnetic spectrum, outer space. Man-made: irrigation system, music, park, seeds, shared knowledge, internet technology, bandwidth, library. The commons is not only nature; digital and knowledge resources count too.

flashcards.front: Name the four MEA (2005) categories of ecosystem services with examples.
flashcards.back: Provisioning (food, water, timber, fuel); regulating (climate, water and air purification, flood control, pollination); cultural (recreation, spiritual, aesthetic); supporting (nutrient cycling, soil formation, photosynthesis; the foundation of the other three). All economic activity depends on them.

flashcards.front: What does the ecosystem-service value chart show (US$ trillion/yr)?
flashcards.back: Spoolman & Miller 2021: coastal marshes/mangroves 24.8 (largest), open ocean 16.3, forests 15.6, grasslands 12.7, coral reefs 9.9, cropland 9.3, marine shelf 5.9, swamps 1.5, lakes/rivers 0.9. Small-area coastal ecosystems give the largest value; natural capital is ignored by conventional accounting.

flashcards.front: List the three ways ecosystem services can be 'paid'.
flashcards.back: 1) Economic: Payment for Ecosystem Services (PES/PJL): beneficiaries pay those who preserve the service, if results are achieved (example Cidanau). 2) Social: mutual consent / joint agreement, as in indigenous communities. 3) Governance: government regulations.

flashcards.front: Explain the Cidanau (Banten) PES case with numbers.
flashcards.back: Priority watershed in Banten. Upstream (Serang, Pandeglang): poor farmers; downstream: industrial Cilegon. Since 2003 the Cidanau Watershed Communication Forum (FKDC) runs an IJL scheme: industries pay Rp1.2-1.75 million per hectare per year to upstream farmers to manage land sustainably.

flashcards.front: Why is the Antarctic ozone hole a global commons example?
flashcards.back: Ozone is a common asset that blocks harmful UV radiation; the 'invisible commons' is unseen but benefits all. In 1985 a 'hole' over Antarctica was found. It endangered human habitats and triggered a global consensus (mutual consent at global scale), leading to the Montreal Protocol. Still monitored.

flashcards.front: Compare the Montreal Protocol and the Kigali Amendment.
flashcards.back: Montreal Protocol (1987): global agreement prohibiting production and use of hazardous ozone-depleting substances, CFCs and derivatives. Kigali Amendment (2016): prohibits HFC, HCFC and similar substances. Example of regulating a global commons by international consensus.

flashcards.front: How does the Subak irrigation system illustrate the commons?
flashcards.back: Bali system of over 1,000 years, UNESCO-listed (about 19,500 ha). Elements: shared water source; multiple users (about 50-400 farmers per source); collective rules on allocation and timing; collective upkeep of canals, dams and water temples; socio-cultural dimension (rituals, Tri Hita Karana).

flashcards.front: Summarise the Dieselgate case and its lesson.
flashcards.back: US Clean Air Act sets strict NOx limits. Volkswagen sold diesels as 'clean technology' but used software that controlled emissions during testing; on the road emissions rose about 20x. NOx forms smog (health issue); millions of vehicles recalled. Lesson: regulation needs monitoring because industry may manipulate compliance.

flashcards.front: List the six elements of a commons arrangement.
flashcards.back: Boundaries (who/where), costs (shared fairly), opportunities for use (how, when, how much), supervision (monitoring), sanctions (clear, progressive) and conflict resolution (mediation, arbitration). Reflect Ostrom's principles; notes add minimal recognition of rights to organise and nested enterprises.

flashcards.front: What were the MDGs, and how do they differ from the SDGs?
flashcards.back: International agreement under UN Sec-Gen Kofi Annan for 2000–2015; adopted by 189 countries, signed by 147 heads of state/government (Millennium Summit, New York, Sept 2000). 8 goals targeting specific/extreme conditions, mostly for developing countries. SDGs: 17 goals, 2015–2030, universal, stronger environmental and intergenerational focus.

flashcards.front: State the key facts of the SDGs (goals, period, who set them).
flashcards.back: 17 interrelated goals for 2015–2030 (the Decade of Action), set by UN member states (192 per slide/quiz) as a global and national commitment; called TPB in Indonesia. Continuation of the MDGs but broader, with stronger emphasis on the environment and intergenerational equity. When adopted, no country had achieved all goals.

flashcards.front: Give the Brundtland definition of sustainable development, its three pillars and two prerequisites.
flashcards.back: Our Common Future (1987): development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (intergenerational equity). Pillars: economic, social, environmental. Global prerequisites: peace and partnership (SDG 16 and 17).

flashcards.front: What numbers define the SDG hierarchy, globally and for Indonesia?
flashcards.back: 17 goals, 169 targets, 231 global indicators; Indonesia uses 289 indicators adapted to national development targets. Each goal splits into targets, each target is measured by indicators. Goals apply to all countries but consider differing conditions and capabilities. IAEG-SDGs reviews the indicators yearly.

flashcards.front: How is Indonesia's SDG commitment anchored in law, and who coordinates it?
flashcards.back: Perpres (Presidential Regulation) No. 59/2017, updated to No. 111/2022 (Roadmap and metadata). A Perpres binds the executive and makes TPB a reference for development planning. Bappenas matches SDG targets and indicators to national development and invites private sector and civil society as partners.

flashcards.front: What is the Voluntary National Review (VNR) and how does Indonesia use it?
flashcards.back: A country's own report on SDG progress presented to the UN (High-Level Political Forum); voluntary, with no enforcement. Indonesia has reported since 2017, about every 2 years, coordinated by the National TPB Secretariat (Bappenas). Themes: 2017 poverty and prosperity, 2019 inclusiveness, 2021 COVID-19 recovery, 2025 inclusive growth.

flashcards.front: Compare Indonesia's performance on SDG 14 and SDG 15.
flashcards.back: Both represent natural capital and biodiversity. SDG 15 (land ecosystems) is consistently declining; SDG 14 (marine ecosystems) is improving and was a focus of the 2017 and 2025 VNRs. This mixed picture motivates IBSAP 2025–2045. Globally about 30% of SDG 14 and 25% of SDG 15 targets were on track (2023).

flashcards.front: What is IBSAP 2025–2045: mission, functions, alignment?
flashcards.back: Indonesia's biodiversity master plan. Mission: protection, sustainable use, enrichment of science and technology (STI), strengthening resources and governance. Functions: national and regional guideline, diplomatic tool in global forums, evaluated every 5 years. Aligned with RPJPN, KM-GBF; mandated by Presidential Instruction 1/2023.

flashcards.front: Define Nature-based Solutions (NbS) per UNEP and IUCN.
flashcards.back: UNEP: actions to protect, conserve, restore, sustainably use and manage natural or modified ecosystems to address social, economic and environmental challenges. IUCN: solutions benefiting people and nature at once. Address climate, food and water security, disaster risk and urban development; a cost-effective route to the SDGs.

flashcards.front: Define Science, Technology and Innovation (STI) as three related areas.
flashcards.back: Science: pursuit of knowledge through systematic study of the physical, natural and social world. Technology: application of knowledge to achieve specific goals. Innovation: a new way of producing, distributing or using goods and services, based on new technology, new business models or new economic or social organisation (not only technological).

flashcards.front: What does the Addis Ababa Action Agenda say about STI?
flashcards.back: The AAAA (2015) is the UN financing and means-of-implementation framework for the 2030 Agenda. STI is one of its Seven Key Actions. Creating and spreading innovations and technologies, including mutually agreed technology transfer, promotes sustainable development, so every country can steer targets toward universal achievement.

flashcards.front: List the four components of the Technology Facilitation Mechanism (TFM) and group them.
flashcards.back: Internal UN bodies monitoring STI in the SDGs: IATT (UN Interagency Task Team) and the 10-Member Group. Communication and knowledge-exchange platforms: the STI Forum (annual multi-stakeholder forum) and 2030 Connect (online platform and information gateway).

flashcards.front: List the three features of STI for SDG achievement.
flashcards.back: 1) Knowledge-centred: generating, disseminating and using knowledge. 2) Goal-specific: each SDG needs different STI (e.g. vaccines for health, renewables for energy). 3) Place-based Priority: each country needs different STI according to its priorities and local context. No one-size-fits-all.

flashcards.front: What did the UN 2023 midpoint reality check find (numbers)?
flashcards.back: Of 140 targets evaluated: 15% progressing per roadmap, 48% not on track, more than 30% stagnant or regressing below the 2015 baseline. Positives: more databases comparable across countries and more agreed methods. Highest on-track share: SDG 12 (~36%). Climate hampers water and energy progress (SDG 6, 7, 11, 13, 14, 15).

flashcards.front: Give gains and lags from the 2026 reality check.
flashcards.back: Gains: 1 billion gained drinking water, 1.2 billion safe sanitation, HIV infections down 30%, electricity 92%, internet 74%, social protection half the world. Lags: 1 in 10 in extreme poverty, 3 billion food insecure, 1.43°C warming by 2025, 273 million children out of school, refugees up by over half. Gaps persist in SDG 1, 5, 10.

flashcards.front: Define climate change and name the main components of the climate system.
flashcards.back: Climate change = long-term change in the average atmospheric conditions shaping local, regional and global climate. Past natural drivers: volcanoes, solar radiation, tectonic shifts, orbital changes. Today's change is extraordinarily fast and primarily human-driven. Climate system components (IPCC 2021): atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere, oceans.

flashcards.front: What are GHGs, and why are they both essential and a problem?
flashcards.back: Gases that absorb heat energy emitted from Earth's surface (<1% of air molecules). Natural greenhouse effect keeps average surface temperature above freezing, so life can exist. Natural: water vapor, CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, ozone. Industrial: CFCs, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆. Excess human emissions enhance the effect and cause global warming.

flashcards.front: What do the GHG concentration data show, and which numbers matter?
flashcards.back: Ice cores (800,000 years): CO₂ stayed roughly 180–300 ppm, then rose sharply after the Industrial Revolution (~1760). CO₂ = 409.9 ppm in 2019 (IPCC); NOAA 2023: CO₂ 419.3 ppm (+50%), CH₄ 1922.6 ppb (+166%), N₂O 336.7 ppb (+25%). CO₂ in ppm, methane in ppb.

flashcards.front: Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect and GWP. Which protocol covers which gases?
flashcards.back: Extra human CO₂/CH₄ enhance the greenhouse effect, so average temperature rises: global warming. GWP = heat a gas traps over a period relative to CO₂ (GWP = 1); N₂O ≈ 298. Kyoto regulates 6 GHGs (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFC, PFC, SF₆). Montreal Protocol covers CFCs (GWP up to ~12,500) and HCFCs (HCFC-22 ≈ 1,800).

flashcards.front: Which gases are GHGs and which are not?
flashcards.back: GHGs: water vapor (H₂O), CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, ozone (O₃); industrial CFCs/HCFCs, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆. NOT GHGs: ammonia (NH₃) and the bulk gases nitrogen (N₂) and oxygen (O₂). Each GHG has a Global Warming Potential (GWP).

flashcards.front: Why can climate change make the SDGs hard to achieve?
flashcards.back: IOC and WMO: climate change can hinder or reverse progress on other SDGs. Weather, climate and water impacts cause slow-onset and fast-onset disasters: temperature rise, sea-level rise, and disruption of land and sea ecosystems. Reality-check framing: SDG 6, 7, 11, 13, 14, 15 are hit. Cambridge (2024) barriers: finance (~48%), greenwashing, marginalised state, top-down intervention, misguided scaling of social enterprise.

flashcards.front: How does SDG 13 (climate) affect the other SDGs, and who is most vulnerable?
flashcards.back: Extreme weather events cause setbacks across health, food, water, cities and livelihoods. COVID-19 cut global GHG emissions by about 6%. Most vulnerable: Small Island Developing States (SIDS), coastal areas, Global South countries, and women, children, youth and other marginalised groups.

flashcards.front: Give examples of how other SDGs contribute to SDG 13.
flashcards.back: SDG 7: renewable transition cuts GHGs. SDG 11: green transport, efficiency, green planning. SDG 12: waste management, less overconsumption, circular economy. SDG 14 & 15: restoring forests, mangroves, marine ecosystems for carbon sequestration. SDG 2: agroforestry, organic fertiliser. About half of emissions stay in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by land and oceans.

flashcards.front: Compare the Paris Agreement (2015) with the Kyoto Protocol (1997), and state Paris's goals.
flashcards.back: Kyoto: top-down targets, developing countries not committed, USA did not join. Paris: all countries set own targets (NDCs). Goals: (1) mitigation, well below 2°C, pursue 1.5°C; (2) adaptation and resilience; (3) align finance flows with low-emission, climate-resilient development. Principles: equity, transparency, sovereignty.

flashcards.front: List the three principles of the Paris Agreement and their mechanisms.
flashcards.back: Equity: CBDR-RC. Transparency: Global Stocktake (GST). Sovereignty: bottom-up architecture with NDCs, each country determines its own level of emissions and reports it as an NDC (its pledge).

flashcards.front: What does CBDR-RC stand for and what does each part mean?
flashcards.back: Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (equity principle; negotiation term 'Right to Development'). Common: all countries contribute to climate change, to varying degrees. Differentiated: 'ability to pay', developed countries commit more. Respective capabilities: support via TFM and funding so all can participate.

flashcards.front: What is the Global Stocktake (GST), which principle does it represent, and what is its aim?
flashcards.back: GST = transparency principle. It assesses how far countries implement their climate commitments (reviews progress) to continually raise ambition and avoid an emergency, e.g. less fossil fuel, more renewables, more climate funding. COP24 added loss and damage and response measures; first GST concluded at COP28 (2023).

flashcards.front: What is Indonesia's climate commitment under Paris?
flashcards.back: Paris ratified as Law No. 16/2016. Keep temperature rise <1.5°C. Net Zero Emission (NZE) by 2060 or earlier. Emission cut targets are split into unconditional (independent) and conditional (with international support); slide 19 lists 29% / 41% for 2030, later updated to 31.89% / 43.2%.

flashcards.front: What numbers does the quiz attach to Indonesia's Enhanced NDC, and what do conditional vs unconditional mean?
flashcards.back: Quiz answer: 31.89% GHG reduction independently (unconditional, domestic effort) and 43.2% with international support (conditional). Slide 19 shows the first NDC as 29% / 41%, and slide 20 shows 31.89% / 43.20% as the 2035 target of the Second NDC, so learn the numbers firmly. Conditional targets depend on finance and technology.

flashcards.front: What is Indonesia's Second NDC (2025) and what are its scenarios?
flashcards.back: Responds to the 1st Global Stocktake. 2035 absolute emission reduction targets: 31.89% unconditional and 43.20% conditional; shift from relative to absolute targets; NZE 2060 or sooner. Scenarios: CPOS (Current Policy), LCCP_Low and LCCP_High (Low Carbon Compatible with Paris).

flashcards.front: What did the 2023 urban heat events in Indonesia show, and what are the impacts?
flashcards.back: BMKG said it was not technically a heat wave, yet the highest temperatures on record (2023) were in Semarang, Surabaya and Makassar. Impacts: heat strain, heat stress, psychosocial disorders and disrupted cognitive performance. Effects differ by socio-economic status.

flashcards.front: Why is air conditioning both an adaptation tool and a risk?
flashcards.back: Adaptation: life-saving in extreme heat, especially for vulnerable groups; maintains quality of life and work productivity. Risk: high energy use and release of HFC refrigerants increase GHGs. Result: potential maladaptation (a vicious cycle), hence the need for sustainable cooling.

flashcards.front: Distinguish direct and indirect emissions from cooling systems.
flashcards.back: Direct: high-GWP refrigerants (CFC, HCFC, HFC) leaking from units or mishandled during servicing. Indirect: energy consumed by cooling, which can reach 50–60% of total energy use in hotels, offices and shopping centres. Measured in CO₂e.

flashcards.front: List the five principles of sustainable cooling.
flashcards.back: (1) Energy savings (efficient equipment, passive design); (2) environmentally friendly refrigerants (zero ODP, low GWP); (3) integration of renewable energy (solar-powered cooling); (4) fair and affordable access (cold storage for traditional fishermen, village cooperatives); (5) circular economy and end-of-life management.

flashcards.front: What does the energy-savings principle of sustainable cooling include?
flashcards.back: Use energy-efficient ACs, refrigerators, freezers, cold storage and chillers, and reduce the thermal load by passive design: effective ventilation, insulation and shading. It targets indirect (energy) emissions.

flashcards.front: What two criteria must a sustainable-cooling refrigerant meet?
flashcards.back: Zero ODP (Ozone Depleting Potential, does not damage the ozone layer) and low GWP (does not contribute to global warming). Problem gases: CFCs, HCFCs and HFCs, whose leakage and servicing cause high direct emissions.

flashcards.front: What is the renewable-energy principle of sustainable cooling?
flashcards.back: Integrate renewable energy into cooling, the named example being solar-powered cooling systems. This lowers indirect emissions from the electricity that cooling consumes.

flashcards.front: What does circular economy and end-of-life management mean for cooling?
flashcards.back: Manage used refrigerants so they are not released directly into the air, and recycle cooling units at end-of-life. Prevents high-GWP CFC/HCFC/HFC leakage after use.

flashcards.front: Rank global GHG emissions by sector in 2019 with their shares.
flashcards.back: Energy 34% (20 GtCO₂-eq) > Industry 24% (14) > AFOLU 22% (13) > Transportation 15% (8.7) > Buildings 6% (3.3). Source: IPCC 2023. About half of AFOLU net emissions are CO₂ from LULUCF, mainly deforestation.

flashcards.front: Define carbon sequestration and give its three types.
flashcards.back: Natural or artificial processes by which CO₂ is removed from the atmosphere or diverted from emission sources, then stored in oceans, terrestrial environments (vegetation, soil, sediments) and geological formations. Types: biological, geological (injected in porous rock), technological (e.g. Direct Air Capture, USD 500–800 per tonne).

flashcards.front: Why do tropical peatlands matter for climate, and how do they form?
flashcards.back: Peatlands cover about 3% of land but store twice as much carbon as all forests. They form where waterlogging limits oxygen so production exceeds decomposition (average depth 5.5–7 m, up to 20 m). A high water table is the key control on decomposition; keeping peat wet is the key lever.

flashcards.front: How does disturbance turn Indonesian peatlands into CO₂ sources?
flashcards.back: Fire, drainage and deforestation release CO₂. Drainage lowers the water table, upper peat turns aerobic, giving 'cold fire': steady CO₂ emission. Dry-season fires (El Niño) give occasional but extensive emissions. Borneo: 26.63 Mha (47.72%) of 55.81 Mha forest logged by 2010.

flashcards.front: What are the AFOLU mitigation strategies, and what is not one?
flashcards.back: AFOLU = Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (22% of 2019 emissions). Strategies: afforestation, reforestation and forest ecosystem restoration; agroforestry; soil carbon management; bioenergy in agriculture. Land clearing by burning is NOT mitigation (it is an emission source).

flashcards.front: What is an SDG spillover? Give an example.
flashcards.back: Effect of a country's policies, practices or trade on other countries' SDG progress; a country can raise its own score while pushing harm abroad. Measured with a footprint approach. Example: importing rice (target 2.1) causes biodiversity loss in the exporter (15.5); palm oil drives deforestation and poor labour conditions (SDG 8).

flashcards.front: What principles underlie SDG interlinkages, and why do rankings mislead?
flashcards.back: SDGs are not achieved one by one; the 2030 Agenda rests on being transformative, universal and indivisible, grounded in systems thinking. Interlinkages show how progress on one target affects others; implementation must be coherent and context-specific. Rankings and linear correlations ignore interlinkages, local context, No One Left Behind and spillovers.

flashcards.front: Define synergy and trade-off between SDGs, with examples.
flashcards.back: Synergy (reinforcing): action gives positive change in both objectives, e.g. clean energy (SDG 7) helping education (4) and health (3). Trade-off (counteracting): positive change in one comes with negative change in another, e.g. agriculture (SDG 2) driving deforestation (15) and water use (6). Aim: maximise synergies, minimise trade-offs.

flashcards.front: List the four activity types and the matching strategy for each.
flashcards.back: Core (synergy; many positive, few negative): scale positive impact. Mixed (significant positive and negative): decouple negatives. Opposed (mainly negative, e.g. coal mining, alcohol, tobacco): transform. Peripheral (insignificant, e.g. cultural preservation): explore ways to add positive impact.

flashcards.front: What are mixed activities? Give the two slide examples.
flashcards.back: Activities with both significant positive and negative SDG impacts. Large-scale agricultural expansion (SDG 2): feeds people but drives deforestation (15), is the largest freshwater user (6), and can widen inequality (10). Renewable energy (SDG 7): energy access but long-term trade-offs such as bird deaths, marine habitat loss, loss of fertile land (SDG 14/15).

flashcards.front: Why can recycling cost more than new material, and what is single vs dual stream?
flashcards.back: Collecting, sorting and cleaning mixed waste is costly. Since 2018 China rejects recyclables below 99% purity (Indonesia and African countries also receive them). Single stream: one container, mixed material qualities. Dual stream: sorted by quality, raising market value. Trade-off: collection convenience vs processing cost and quality.

flashcards.front: How does technology use affect SDG 12, and what does the inverted-U curve show?
flashcards.back: Development and technology use raise material and environmental footprints, hindering SDG 12 (targets 12.2 and 8.4). Inverted-U: per capita material footprint rises with per capita income until a turning point, then falls (decoupling). Examples: IKN construction materials, 12 coal power plants. This is the T of IPAT.

flashcards.front: Compare SDG synergies in the Global North and South (Boar et al. 2021).
flashcards.back: Global North: synergies include all three dimensions (social, economic, environmental); new technology and renewable energy reduce environmental impact. Global South: synergies cover only one dimension, so gains in one area often come at others' expense. North's synergies may partly rely on outsourcing impacts through spillovers.

flashcards.front: Define the nexus approach and its principles.
flashcards.back: Deepens integration between goals and targets across sectors, avoids unsustainable and inefficient conflicts and overlaps, and strengthens synergies while reducing trade-offs. Principles: ensure access to resources for vulnerable groups, promote efficient use of resources, ensure sustainability. Countries prioritise SDGs by local context.

flashcards.front: What is the Food–Energy–Water nexus and which SDGs sit at its core?
flashcards.back: Food, energy and water interact and affect the SDGs yet are often managed separately: food needs water and energy, energy needs water and land, water needs energy. Inner ring of the SDG wheel: SDG 2 (food), 6 (water), 7 (energy); managing it well ripples to all 17 SDGs.

flashcards.front: Name and group the nine reasons for a FEW nexus approach.
flashcards.back: A. Basic needs/scarcity: limited access, increasing demand, limited resources. B. Global/environmental: global goods (traded internationally), regional differences, interdependence with climate and environmental change. C. Security/governance: security (a crisis causes instability), tightly regulated markets, identification and management of risks.
